records.title: The Fresnel equations: one interface
records.summary: Reflection and transmission of a plane wave at a single planar interface, derived from the two boundary conditions: Snell's law, the Fresnel coefficients for s and p polarization and their phases, the power coefficients and why T is not |t|², the Brewster angle, total internal reflection and the evanescent wave, absorbing media and the branch of the complex angle, and the ellipsometric ratio ρ = r_p / r_s.

references.cite: M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §1.5 and §14.2
J. D. Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 1999), §7.3–7.4
R. M. A. Azzam and N. M. Bashara, Ellipsometry and Polarized Light (North-Holland, 1977), ch. 4
F. Goos and H. Hänchen, Ann. Phys. 436, 333 (1947)
S. J. Byrnes, Multilayer optical calculations, arXiv:1603.02720 (2016)

records.body:
Every thin-film calculation is built from one event repeated: a plane wave meets a flat boundary between two
homogeneous media and splits into a reflected and a transmitted wave. Everything in this chapter follows from the
continuity of the tangential components of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ at that boundary (the
[Foundations](learn/common/maxwell-and-boundary-conditions.html)), applied once. The algebra is short, and worth
doing once in full, because the same two equations, with Bessel functions in place of exponentials, give Mie's
coefficients for a sphere and the cylinder's.

## Snell's law

A wave in medium 1 (index $n_1$) arrives at angle $\theta_1$ from the normal. Its field varies along the interface as
$e^{i k_0 n_1 \sin\theta_1\, x}$, and the boundary conditions must hold at every $x$, so the reflected and transmitted
waves carry the same in-plane wavenumber $k_x = k_0 n_1\sin\theta_1$. That alone fixes the directions:

$$
n_1 \sin\theta_1 = n_2 \sin\theta_2 ,
$$

and the reflected wave leaves at $\theta_1$. The quantity $n \sin\theta$ is conserved through any stack of parallel
layers, which is why a multilayer can be solved layer by layer at a single $k_x$, and why an angle of incidence is best
thought of as an in-plane wavenumber: every layer's normal wavenumber follows as $k_{z,j} = k_0\sqrt{n_j^2 - n_1^2\sin^2\theta_1}$,
real or imaginary.

## Two polarizations, two sets of coefficients

The field is split into the part polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence (**s**, or TE, from the German
*senkrecht*) and the part polarized in it (**p**, or TM). They do not mix at a planar interface, because the
boundary conditions never couple a field component along $y$ to one in the $xz$ plane. For s polarization,
$\mathbf{E} = E_y\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, and the tangential $\mathbf{H}$ is $H_x \propto n\cos\theta\, E_y$ (from
$\nabla\times\mathbf{E} = i\omega\mu_0\mathbf{H}$). Continuity of $E_y$ and of $H_x$ at $z = 0$ gives, with the
incident amplitude 1,

$$
1 + r_s = t_s, \qquad n_1\cos\theta_1\,(1 - r_s) = n_2\cos\theta_2\, t_s ,
$$

two equations for two unknowns. For p polarization the roles swap: $\mathbf{H} = H_y\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is continuous,
and the tangential $E_x \propto (\cos\theta/n)\,H_y$. Solving both pairs,

$$
r_s = \frac{n_1\cos\theta_1 - n_2\cos\theta_2}{n_1\cos\theta_1 + n_2\cos\theta_2},
\qquad
r_p = \frac{n_2\cos\theta_1 - n_1\cos\theta_2}{n_2\cos\theta_1 + n_1\cos\theta_2},
$$

$$
t_s = \frac{2 n_1\cos\theta_1}{n_1\cos\theta_1 + n_2\cos\theta_2},
\qquad
t_p = \frac{2 n_1\cos\theta_1}{n_2\cos\theta_1 + n_1\cos\theta_2}.
$$

Both have the same structure, $(\eta_1 - \eta_2)/(\eta_1 + \eta_2)$ in terms of a **tilted admittance**,
$\eta = n\cos\theta$ for s and $\eta = n/\cos\theta$ for p (up to the convention for $r_p$). That one observation is
the whole thin-film theory in a nutshell: the [transfer matrix](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html) carries nothing but
these admittances from layer to layer.

**The sign of $r_p$.** Two conventions are in use for the direction of the p-polarized electric field, and they
differ in the sign of $r_p$; the expression above, in which $r_p \to r_s$ at normal incidence, follows Byrnes (2016),
whose transfer-matrix code PyStratify's planar engine extends. In the other convention (Born and Wolf) $r_p$ changes
sign, so that $r_p = -r_s$ at normal incidence. Nothing physical depends on the choice, but the phase $\Delta$ of
ellipsometry does, by 180°, and comparing two codes or a code with a paper starts with settling it.

**Phases.** For external reflection ($n_1 < n_2$) below the Brewster angle, $r_s$ is negative: the s wave flips its
phase by $\pi$ on reflection from a denser medium, the origin of the "half-wave loss" of elementary optics, while
$r_p$ in this convention is positive and crosses zero at Brewster. Internal reflection reverses both signs.

## Power coefficients

The reflected and incident waves travel in the same medium, so the reflectance is simply $R = |r|^2$. The
transmitted wave travels in a different medium at a different angle, and the ratio of the power flows *normal to
the interface* carries the ratio of the admittances:

$$
R = |r|^2, \qquad
T_s = \frac{\mathrm{Re}\,(n_2\cos\theta_2)}{\mathrm{Re}\,(n_1\cos\theta_1)}\,|t_s|^2,
\qquad
T_p = \frac{\mathrm{Re}\,(n_2\cos\theta_2^{*})}{\mathrm{Re}\,(n_1\cos\theta_1^{*})}\,|t_p|^2 .
$$

$T = |t|^2$ is a common mistake; it fails already at normal incidence between two dielectrics, where
$|t|^2 = 4n_1^2/(n_1+n_2)^2$ is not $1 - R$. The conjugates in $T_p$ matter only for absorbing media, where the
Poynting vector of an inhomogeneous wave is not along the real part of the wavevector. With them, $R + T = 1$ holds
exactly for lossless media, which is the first of the [Verification](verification.html) page's checks. At normal
incidence both polarizations reduce to

$$
R = \left(\frac{n_2 - n_1}{n_2 + n_1}\right)^2 ,
$$

4 % for glass in air, 31 % for silicon ($n \approx 3.9$), 1.3 % for a water surface.

::: example fresnel-air-glass

## The Brewster angle

$r_p$ vanishes where $n_2\cos\theta_1 = n_1\cos\theta_2$, which with Snell's law is $\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90°$: the
reflected and transmitted directions are perpendicular. The dipoles driven in medium 2 oscillate along the transmitted
$\mathbf{E}$, which is then exactly along the would-be reflected ray, and a dipole does not radiate along its own
axis. This happens at

$$
\tan\theta_B = \frac{n_2}{n_1},
$$

56.3° for glass in air, 75.6° for silicon. Light reflected at the Brewster angle is purely s-polarized, which is how
polarizing sunglasses cut glare and how Brewster windows keep a laser cavity lossless for one polarization. For an
absorbing medium $r_p$ never reaches zero; its minimum defines a **pseudo-Brewster angle**, which for metals lies
near 70–80° and is where ellipsometers measure, because the phase difference between $r_p$ and $r_s$ changes fastest
there.

## Total internal reflection and the evanescent wave

From the dense side ($n_1 > n_2$), Snell's law has no real solution beyond the critical angle

$$
\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1},
$$

41.8° for glass to air. There $\cos\theta_2 = i\sqrt{n_1^2\sin^2\theta_1/n_2^2 - 1}$ becomes imaginary: the
transmitted field is $e^{ik_x x}e^{-\kappa z}$, bound to the interface and decaying into medium 2 with

$$
\frac{1}{\kappa} = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\sqrt{n_1^2\sin^2\theta_1 - n_2^2}} ,
$$

about a fifth of a wavelength a few degrees past the critical angle, growing without bound as $\theta_1 \to \theta_c$.
Both reflection coefficients have unit modulus, $|r_s| = |r_p| = 1$, so all the power returns; what is not zero is
their **phase**, which differs between s and p and depends on the angle. That phase is a design quantity in its own
right: the Fresnel rhomb turns linear into circular polarization with two total reflections at the angle where the
s–p phase difference is 45°, with no birefringent material at all. The phase also varies with $k_x$, and a beam of
finite width, a superposition of plane waves with slightly different $k_x$, is shifted sideways along the interface
by a fraction of a wavelength on reflection: the Goos–Hänchen shift (1947), measured with a multiply reflecting
glass block.

The evanescent field still reaches a fraction of a wavelength into the second medium, and it carries no power only as
long as nothing is there to take it. A second dense medium brought that close lets light tunnel through (frustrated
total reflection, the optical analogue of quantum tunnelling and the principle of the beam-splitter cube), a molecule
there is excited (total-internal-reflection fluorescence microscopy), and a metal film couples it to surface
plasmons, the principle of the [Kretschmann configuration](learn/films/surface-plasmon-resonance.html).

::: example fresnel-glass-air

## Absorbing media and the branch of the square root

For an absorbing medium the index is complex, $\tilde n = n + ik$ (time dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$, $k \ge 0$), and
so is $\cos\theta_2 = \sqrt{1 - n_1^2\sin^2\theta_1/\tilde n_2^2}$. The angle $\theta_2$ then has no geometric
meaning: the planes of constant phase and of constant amplitude in medium 2 are not parallel (an *inhomogeneous*
wave), and the transmitted wave decays along $z$ whatever its direction. The square root has two branches, and the
physical one is the wave that carries power away from the interface and decays into the medium, that is
$\mathrm{Re}(\tilde n_2\cos\theta_2) > 0$ or, at the boundary of that condition, $\mathrm{Im}(\tilde n_2\cos\theta_2) > 0$.
A code that takes the principal square root blindly gets this wrong for some metals and for every evanescent wave
beyond the critical angle in a weakly absorbing medium; Byrnes's implementation tests the branch explicitly, and
PyStratify's planar engine inherits the test. Once the branch is right, every formula above holds unchanged for
metals, for semiconductors above their band gap and for evanescent waves alike, which is why one engine serves a
glass lens, a silver mirror and a surface-plasmon sensor.

## Ellipsometry: the ratio of the two

The two Fresnel coefficients are rarely measured separately. An ellipsometer sends in light of known polarization
and measures the polarization of the reflected light, that is the complex ratio

$$
\rho = \frac{r_p}{r_s} = \tan\Psi\, e^{i\Delta} ,
$$

$\tan\Psi$ being the amplitude ratio and $\Delta$ the phase difference. For a bare substrate $\rho$ inverts in closed
form to the complex index,

$$
\tilde n_2 = n_1 \sin\theta_1\sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{1 - \rho}{1 + \rho}\right)^2 \tan^2\theta_1} ,
$$

which is how the optical constants of most materials in the databases were first obtained, and for a film on a
substrate $\rho$ follows from the transfer matrix and is fitted for thickness and index (Azzam and Bashara). The
calculator's Ψ and Δ are this ratio with the sign convention $\rho = -r_p/r_s$, which puts $\Delta$ in the range
ellipsometer software reports; the 180° difference between conventions is the one to remember when comparing with a
paper.

records.title: The transfer matrix: a stack of thin films
records.summary: Abelès' characteristic matrix of a layer, derived from the two boundary conditions; how a stack multiplies them; the admittance that gives R and T and Macleod's admittance locus; the amplitude form with interface and propagation matrices that also gives the field inside; quarter-wave and half-wave layers and Herpin's equivalent layer; and the numerics: growing exponentials, the scattering-matrix alternative, and what PyStratify does.

references.cite: F. Abelès, Ann. Phys. (Paris) 12, 596 (1950)
H. A. Macleod, Thin-Film Optical Filters, 3rd ed. (Institute of Physics Publishing, 2001), ch. 2–3
M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §1.6
P. Yeh, Optical Waves in Layered Media (Wiley, 1988), ch. 5
A. Herpin, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 225, 182 (1947)
L. Li, J. Opt. Soc. Am. A 13, 1024 (1996)
S. J. Byrnes, Multilayer optical calculations, arXiv:1603.02720 (2016)

records.body:
Between two interfaces a wave travels back and forth, picking up phase on each pass, and every reflection spawns
another. Summing those multiple reflections term by term is possible for one layer (it gives the Airy formula of the
[Fabry–Pérot](learn/films/fabry-perot-etalons.html) section) and impractical for twenty. The transfer matrix does
the bookkeeping instead: in each layer the field is a forward and a backward wave, and a $2\times 2$ matrix carries
either the two amplitudes or the two tangential fields from one side of the layer to the other. The
[Foundations](learn/common/why-transfer-matrices.html) chapter explains why such a matrix must exist for any
stratified geometry; this section writes it out for films, the way Abelès did in 1950, and shows what it is good for.

## The characteristic matrix of a layer

Take s polarization (p differs only in the admittance) and a layer $j$ of index $n_j$ and thickness $d_j$ at the
in-plane wavenumber $k_x = k_0 n_0\sin\theta_0$ fixed by the incidence. Inside the layer the field is
$E_y(z) = a\,e^{ik_z z} + b\,e^{-ik_z z}$ with $k_z = k_0 n_j\cos\theta_j$, and the tangential magnetic field, in
units that make the admittance of free space 1, is $H_x(z) = \eta_j\,(a\,e^{ik_z z} - b\,e^{-ik_z z})$ with the
**tilted admittance** $\eta_j = n_j\cos\theta_j$. Eliminate $a$ and $b$ between the values at the two faces, a
distance $d_j$ apart, and the result is a matrix relation between the tangential fields themselves:

$$
\begin{pmatrix} E \\ H \end{pmatrix}_{\text{front}} =
\begin{pmatrix} \cos\delta_j & \dfrac{i}{\eta_j}\sin\delta_j \\[4pt] i\,\eta_j \sin\delta_j & \cos\delta_j \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} E \\ H \end{pmatrix}_{\text{back}},
\qquad
\delta_j = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\, n_j d_j \cos\theta_j ,
$$

Abelès' **characteristic matrix** $M_j$, with the phase thickness $\delta_j$ and, for p polarization,
$\eta_j = n_j/\cos\theta_j$. Its determinant is 1 (it is a product of two matrices of unit Wronskian), its trace is
$2\cos\delta_j$, and it depends on the layer through $\delta_j$ and $\eta_j$ only: two numbers per layer per
wavelength, which is why a stack of forty layers is no harder than one.

## A stack and its admittance

The tangential fields are continuous at every interface, so what leaves the back of layer $j$ enters the front of
layer $j+1$ unchanged, and the matrices of successive layers simply multiply. In the substrate there is only a
transmitted wave, whose fields are in the ratio $H/E = \eta_s$, so for $q$ layers on a substrate

$$
\begin{pmatrix} B \\ C \end{pmatrix} = \left(\prod_{j=1}^{q} M_j\right) \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \eta_s \end{pmatrix},
\qquad Y = \frac{C}{B} .
$$

$Y$ is the **admittance of the whole stack**: seen from the incident medium of admittance $\eta_0$, the coated
substrate behaves exactly like a single surface of admittance $Y$, and the single-interface formulas of the
[Fresnel section](learn/films/fresnel-equations.html) apply to it:

$$
r = \frac{\eta_0 - Y}{\eta_0 + Y}, \qquad R = |r|^2, \qquad
T = \frac{4\,\eta_0\,\mathrm{Re}\,\eta_s}{|\eta_0 B + C|^2}, \qquad A = 1 - R - T .
$$

This is the formulation of Macleod's book and of coating design in general, and its power is that $Y$ can be followed
layer by layer. Macleod's **admittance locus** plots $Y$ in the complex plane as each layer is added: a lossless
layer moves $Y$ along a circle centred on the real axis, through an angle $2\delta$, and a design is a path from
$\eta_s$ to the target $Y = \eta_0$ (zero reflectance) or as far from it as possible (a mirror). A designer reads
off from the diagram which layer to add next and how thick, which is how the classic antireflection and filter
designs below were found long before computers.

## The amplitude form: the field inside

The same physics can be written for the wave amplitudes instead of the fields, which is what Byrnes's code and
PyStratify's planar engine do. Crossing an interface between media $i$ and $j$ maps the forward and backward
amplitudes by an **interface matrix** built from the Fresnel coefficients, and crossing a layer by a diagonal
**propagation matrix**:

$$
\begin{pmatrix} a_i \\ b_i \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{t_{ij}}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & r_{ij} \\ r_{ij} & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a_j \\ b_j \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
P_j = \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\delta_j} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{i\delta_j} \end{pmatrix} .
$$

The product $\tilde M = I_{01} P_1 I_{12} P_2 \cdots I_{q s}$ relates the incident-medium amplitudes $(1, r)$ to the
substrate's $(t, 0)$, so $r = \tilde M_{21}/\tilde M_{11}$ and $t = 1/\tilde M_{11}$. The two forms are equivalent
(a change of basis in each layer), but the amplitude form hands over the forward and backward amplitudes in every
layer as a by-product. From them the field at any depth,

$$
E_y(z) = a_j e^{ik_{z,j}(z - z_j)} + b_j e^{-ik_{z,j}(z - z_j)} ,
$$

is a one-line evaluation, and the power absorbed in layer $j$ is the difference of the Poynting flux through its two
faces, the per-layer absorptance of the [solar-cell section](learn/films/solar-cell-absorption.html). The
calculator's field profile and layer absorptances come from exactly these amplitudes.

## Quarter waves and half waves

Two thicknesses make the characteristic matrix trivial at the design wavelength $\lambda_0$, at normal incidence:

- a **half-wave** layer ($n d = \lambda_0/2$, $\delta = \pi$) has $M = -I$: it is *absent*, and the stack reflects
  as if it were not there (which is why the spacer of a [bandpass filter](learn/films/bandpass-filters.html) is a
  half wave);
- a **quarter-wave** layer ($n d = \lambda_0/4$, $\delta = \pi/2$) has $M = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & i/\eta \\ i\eta & 0
  \end{pmatrix}$ and turns an admittance $Y$ into $\eta^2/Y$: an *admittance transformer*, the optical
  quarter-wave line.

A single quarter-wave layer of index $n_1$ on a substrate $n_s$ therefore presents $Y = n_1^2/n_s$ and gives

$$
R = \left(\frac{n_0 n_s - n_1^2}{n_0 n_s + n_1^2}\right)^2 ,
$$

which vanishes for $n_1 = \sqrt{n_0 n_s}$, 1.23 for glass in air. No durable material has so low an index; magnesium
fluoride (1.38) comes closest, and leaves about 1.3 % instead of 4 %.

::: example quarter-wave-ar

The minimum sits at $\lambda_0 = 4 n_1 d$ and is broad, because $\delta$ changes slowly with $\lambda$. Two or three
layers (the V-coat and the quarter–half–quarter design) broaden it further, and a graded index takes the idea to its
limit in the [moth-eye antireflection](learn/films/moth-eye-antireflection.html) section.

**Herpin's equivalent layer.** Any symmetric combination of layers, $p\,q\,p$ say, has a characteristic matrix of the
same form as a single layer, with an *equivalent* index and phase thickness that depend on wavelength (Herpin 1947;
Macleod ch. 6). A combination of two available materials can therefore stand in for an index that no material
offers, including the 1.23 above, and a periodic stack is a periodic repetition of one equivalent layer, which is the
shortest route to the stop band of the [Bragg mirror](learn/films/bragg-mirrors.html). The equivalent index becomes
imaginary exactly inside the stop band.

## Oblique incidence and absorbing layers

Nothing above assumes normal incidence or real indices. At an angle, $\cos\theta_j$ shortens each layer's phase
thickness, so every feature of a spectrum moves to shorter wavelengths as the coating is tilted, and the admittances
of s and p separate, so the two polarizations respond differently (the p admittance $n/\cos\theta$ grows with angle,
the s admittance shrinks). In an absorbing layer $\delta_j$ is complex, $\cos\delta_j$ and $\sin\delta_j$ become
hyperbolic, and the wave decays across the layer; the formulas stay valid, and $A = 1 - R - T$ is now positive.

## Numerics: where the matrix overflows, and what to do

For a thick absorbing layer, or an evanescent one beyond the critical angle, $e^{i\delta_j}$ contains a real
exponential $e^{\mathrm{Im}\,\delta_j}$ that grows without bound: 10 µm of a metal at visible wavelengths gives
$e^{+700}$, beyond double precision. The characteristic matrix carries both $e^{+}$ and $e^{-}$ and overflows, and
even before that the reflected amplitude is the small difference of two huge numbers. Three remedies are in use:

1. **Propagate only decaying waves.** Byrnes's formulation orders the exponentials so that the growing one never
   appears in a product that is later subtracted, and clamps a layer beyond which nothing returns as opaque; this is
   what `pystratify.planar` does, and it is why the calculator can hold a millimetre of metal.
2. **The scattering matrix.** Instead of transfer matrices, combine the reflection and transmission matrices of
   sub-stacks with Redheffer's star product. Every quantity is then a reflection or transmission coefficient, bounded
   by one for a passive stack, and no exponential ever grows (Li 1996, who proved the stability). PyStratify's
   [Verification](verification.html) page compares the planar engine with an independent scattering-matrix solver on
   lossy, oblique and opaque stacks to $10^{-10}$.
3. **Logarithmic amplitudes.** Carry $\log a_j$ and $\log b_j$ rather than $a_j$ and $b_j$, so that a factor
   $e^{700}$ is the number 700; this is how PyStratify's sphere and cylinder solvers stay stable to any thickness and
   order, as the [multilayered sphere](learn/spheres/recursive-transfer-matrix.html) section describes.

The second trap is subtler: the **branch of $\cos\theta_j$** in an absorbing or evanescent layer. Taking the wrong
sign makes the "forward" wave grow into the layer, and the error does not announce itself; it shows up as $R > 1$ or
as $T$ failing to vanish beyond the critical angle. The forward-decaying branch of the
[Fresnel section](learn/films/fresnel-equations.html) must be chosen in every layer, and the energy-conservation
checks ($R + T = 1$ below and beyond the critical angle for lossless stacks) are the tests that catch a wrong branch.

records.title: Coherence and thick substrates
records.summary: Why a thin film draws interference fringes and a millimetre-thick substrate does not: the coherence length and the fringe spacing, the incoherent sum of intensities derived as a phase average, the intensity transfer matrix that joins coherent sub-stacks through incoherent layers, the asymmetry R ≠ R′ of an absorbing film, partial coherence, and what a spectrometer actually records.

references.cite: C. C. Katsidis and D. I. Siapkas, Appl. Opt. 41, 3978 (2002)
B. Harbecke, Appl. Phys. B 39, 165 (1986)
C. L. Mitsas and D. I. Siapkas, Appl. Opt. 34, 1678 (1995)
M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §7.6 and ch. 10
S. J. Byrnes, Multilayer optical calculations, arXiv:1603.02720 (2016)

records.body:
The transfer matrix adds amplitudes: every reflected wave interferes with every other. That is right for a film a few
hundred nanometres thick, and wrong for the glass it sits on. A 1 mm plate in a spectrometer shows no fringes, though
the matrix predicts them, with a contrast of nearly 8 % for glass. The discrepancy is not a failure of Maxwell's
equations; it is a statement about the light and the instrument, and once it is made precise it becomes a second
$2\times 2$ formalism, this time for intensities, that joins seamlessly to the first.

## Fringes too fine to see

Two reflections that differ by a path $2 n d \cos\theta$ interfere only if the light stays coherent over that path.
A source of bandwidth $\Delta\lambda$ has a coherence length

$$
\ell_c \approx \frac{\lambda^2}{\Delta\lambda},
$$

30 µm for a 10 nm bandwidth at 550 nm. Put the other way, the fringes of a slab are spaced by

$$
\Delta\lambda_\text{fringe} = \frac{\lambda^2}{2 n d \cos\theta},
$$

which for 1 mm of glass at 600 nm is 0.12 nm. Any instrument with a coarser resolution, nearly all of them, averages
over many fringes and records their mean. Three other averages act in the same direction: a real plate varies in
thickness by more than a wavelength across the beam, the beam has a spread of angles (a cone of a few degrees
already smears $\cos\theta$ by more than a fringe), and a thermal source's phase is random on a timescale set by its
bandwidth. Each of them averages the phase $\delta = 2\pi n d\cos\theta/\lambda$ uniformly over $2\pi$, and that is
the operational definition of an **incoherent layer**: one whose round-trip phase is, as far as the measurement can
tell, uniformly random.

## Adding intensities: the phase average

Take the Airy sum for a slab, $t = t_{12}t_{21}e^{i\delta}/(1 - r_{21}^2 e^{2i\delta})$, and average $|t|^2$ over
$\delta$. The cross terms between passes with different numbers of round trips carry $e^{2im\delta}$, $m \ne 0$, and
average to zero; what survives is the sum of the powers of the individual passes,

$$
\langle T \rangle_\delta = T_{12}\,T_{21}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} R_{21}^{2m} = \frac{T_{12}T_{21}}{1 - R_{21}^2},
$$

a geometric series in powers, not amplitudes. For a bare, non-absorbing plate with face reflectance
$R_0 = \left(\frac{n - 1}{n + 1}\right)^2$ this gives

$$
R = R_0 + \frac{(1 - R_0)^2 R_0}{1 - R_0^2} = \frac{2R_0}{1 + R_0}, \qquad T = \frac{1 - R_0}{1 + R_0} ,
$$

8.2 % and 91.8 % for glass: twice the single-surface loss, less a little. The phase average and the "add
intensities" rule are the same statement; PyStratify's [Verification](verification.html) page checks the engine's
incoherent path against an explicit average of coherent solves over the layer's phase, and they agree to $10^{-9}$.

## Coherent films on incoherent plates

Harbecke (1986), Mitsas and Siapkas (1995) and Katsidis and Siapkas (2002) generalised this to any stack. The layers
are grouped into **coherent sub-stacks**, each solved with the transfer matrix of amplitudes, which yields its
reflectance and transmittance from the front, $R$, $T$, and from the back, $R'$, $T'$. The sub-stacks are then joined
through the incoherent layers by $2\times 2$ **intensity matrices**: for a sub-stack between two incoherent regions

$$
\mathcal{I} = \frac{1}{T}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -R' \\ R & T T' - R R' \end{pmatrix},
$$

which carries the forward and backward *powers* across it exactly as the characteristic matrix carries the fields,
and the propagation through an incoherent layer of absorptance is a diagonal matrix of its single-pass attenuation
$e^{\mp 2\,\mathrm{Im}\,\delta}$. A thin film on a thick substrate is then exact for both: the film's fringes survive,
and the substrate contributes its two faces in power. Two features of the formula deserve notice. **$R \ne R'$** for
an absorbing sub-stack (a dielectric film on an absorbing one reflects differently from the two sides, though
$T = T'$ always, by reciprocity), so the back-side coefficients cannot be dropped. And an incoherent layer's own
thickness enters only through its absorption: a lossless incoherent plate's thickness has no effect on $R$ and $T$ at
all, which is why a measured spectrum cannot tell a 1 mm plate from a 2 mm one.

PyStratify's planar engine implements this scheme (Byrnes's `inc_tmm`); in the calculator each layer carries a
coherence flag (*c* or *i*), the substrate behind the last layer is semi-infinite, and a thick substrate is written
as an incoherent layer followed by air.

::: example film-on-thick-glass

At the film's half-wave wavelength it is absent, and the reflectance returns to the bare plate's $2R_0/(1 + R_0)$.
Between those points the film's fringes ride on the plate's incoherent background, which is what a measured spectrum
looks like. A coherent calculation of the same stack would show the film's fringes modulated by a comb of 0.12 nm
fringes of nearly 8 % depth, and would have to be computed on a grid finer than 0.03 nm to resolve them at all,
which is the practical reason the incoherent treatment matters even when the instrument's resolution is known.

## Partial coherence

Between the two limits sit rough interfaces, thickness gradients and finite spectral resolution, which damp fringes
without removing them. Three models are in use, and each is a different average of the coherent result:

- **spectral resolution**: convolve the coherent spectrum with the instrument's line shape; exact for a perfect
  plane-parallel plate measured with a known slit, and the right model for a thin wafer in a high-resolution FTIR,
  where the fringes of 500 µm of silicon are resolved and routinely used to measure thickness;
- **thickness variation**: average the coherent result over the distribution of $d$ across the beam, which damps the
  fringes by the Fourier transform of that distribution; a Gaussian spread of $\sigma_d$ multiplies the fringe
  contrast by $\exp[-2(2\pi n\sigma_d/\lambda)^2]$;
- **phase averaging within a layer**, Katsidis and Siapkas' formulation, in which a layer is assigned a degree of
  coherence between 0 and 1 that interpolates between the amplitude and the intensity matrices.

Their infrared reflectance of a thin film on a thick wafer is the textbook case of fringes riding on an incoherent
background, with the semi-infinite and the finite incoherent substrate side by side.

::: classic katsidis-2002

## What the model is not

An incoherent layer is a model of the measurement, not of the light inside the plate: the fields in the glass are as
coherent as anywhere else, and a different instrument (a laser and a photodiode, say) would see the fringes. The
treatment also assumes the incoherent layer is thick enough for the multiply reflected beams to be laterally
separated or phase-randomised; a layer of a few wavelengths that is simply rough belongs to the scattering models of
the [textured surfaces](learn/films/textured-surfaces.html) section. And a stack with *several* incoherent layers is
handled exactly by the intensity matrices, but the engine's only independent check for that case is the explicit
phase average, as the Verification page states.

records.title: Bragg mirrors: periodic stacks and stop bands
records.summary: A quarter-wave stack of two materials reflects almost perfectly over a band of wavelengths: the peak reflectance from the admittance, Bloch's theorem and the dispersion relation of the one-dimensional crystal, the stop band width from the index contrast, the N-period reflectance through Chebyshev polynomials, penetration depth, higher-order bands and the ones that vanish, oblique incidence and the omnidirectional mirror.

references.cite: P. Yeh, A. Yariv and C.-S. Hong, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 67, 423 (1977)
P. Yeh, Optical Waves in Layered Media (Wiley, 1988), ch. 6
H. A. Macleod, Thin-Film Optical Filters, 3rd ed. (Institute of Physics Publishing, 2001), ch. 5
M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §1.6.5
D. I. Babic and S. W. Corzine, IEEE J. Quantum Electron. 28, 514 (1992)
Y. Fink et al., Science 282, 1679 (1998)
J. N. Winn, Y. Fink, S. Fan and J. D. Joannopoulos, Opt. Lett. 23, 1573 (1998)

records.body:
Alternate a high index $n_H$ and a low index $n_L$, each a quarter wave thick at $\lambda_0$, and the reflections from
every interface return in phase: the wave reflected at an H→L boundary has the opposite sign to the one reflected at
an L→H boundary, and the quarter-wave round trip adds another $\pi$, so all of them add. With enough periods the stack
reflects nearly everything over a band around $\lambda_0$: a dielectric mirror with no absorption, the basis of laser
mirrors, of distributed Bragg reflectors in VCSELs, and the one-dimensional photonic crystal. Yeh, Yariv and Hong's
1977 paper is the one that treats it as a crystal, and this section follows them.

## The peak: quarter waves in series

At $\lambda_0$ each quarter-wave layer maps an admittance $Y$ onto $n^2/Y$ (see
[the transfer matrix](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html)). Starting from the substrate $n_s$, a pair L then H
multiplies it by $(n_H/n_L)^2$, so $N$ pairs, high index outermost, present

$$
Y = \left(\frac{n_H}{n_L}\right)^{2N} n_s ,
\qquad
R(\lambda_0) = \left(\frac{n_0 - Y}{n_0 + Y}\right)^2 .
$$

$Y$ grows geometrically with $N$, so $1 - R$ falls geometrically, by the factor $(n_L/n_H)^4$ per pair once
$Y \gg n_0$: eight pairs of TiO₂-like and SiO₂-like layers (2.3 and 1.45) already reach 99.84 %, and eleven pairs
99.99 %. Ending the stack with a low-index layer instead divides $Y$ by $n_L^2$ and lowers the peak; the outermost
layer should be the one of higher admittance contrast with the incident medium. For a VCSEL mirror in GaAs/AlAs
(3.5/2.9, a contrast of only 1.2) the same 99.9 % needs about thirty pairs, which is why such mirrors are grown
rather than evaporated.

## The band: Bloch waves and the dispersion relation

An infinite periodic stack is a one-dimensional crystal, and Bloch's theorem says its eigenwaves reproduce
themselves from one period to the next up to a phase: $E(z + \Lambda) = e^{iK\Lambda}E(z)$, with $K$ the Bloch
wavenumber. The characteristic matrix $M$ of one period (the product $M_H M_L$) must therefore have the eigenvalue
$e^{iK\Lambda}$, and since $\det M = 1$ the two eigenvalues are $e^{\pm iK\Lambda}$, whose sum is the trace:

$$
\cos K\Lambda = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Tr}\,M
= \cos\delta_H\cos\delta_L - \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\eta_H}{\eta_L} + \frac{\eta_L}{\eta_H}\right)\sin\delta_H\sin\delta_L .
$$

This is the **dispersion relation** of the crystal. Where the right-hand side lies between $-1$ and $1$, $K$ is real
and the wave propagates; where it exceeds 1 in magnitude, $K$ is complex, the Bloch wave decays as
$e^{-|\mathrm{Im}\,K| z}$, and a thick enough stack reflects it completely. That decaying range is the **stop band**;
its edges are where $\cos K\Lambda = \pm 1$. For a quarter-wave stack at normal incidence, $\delta_H = \delta_L =
\delta$ and the condition $|\cos 2\delta - \ldots| = 1$ gives a band centred on $\delta = \pi/2$ with a full width, in the
relative wavenumber $g = \lambda_0/\lambda$, of

$$
\Delta g = \frac{4}{\pi}\arcsin\!\left(\frac{n_H - n_L}{n_H + n_L}\right),
$$

about 0.29 for 2.3/1.45, or 524–702 nm around 600 nm, and 0.11 for GaAs/AlAs. The width depends on the index contrast
alone; the period count only decides how close to 1 the reflectance gets inside the band and how sharp its edges
are. Inside the band the imaginary part of $K$ is largest at the centre, $|\mathrm{Im}\,K|\Lambda \approx
2(n_H - n_L)/(n_H + n_L)$ for small contrast, which gives the number of periods the field penetrates.

## N periods exactly: Chebyshev polynomials

For a finite stack of $N$ periods Yeh, Yariv and Hong evaluate $M^N$ in closed form through the Chebyshev
polynomials of the second kind, $U_N(\cos K\Lambda) = \sin[(N+1)K\Lambda]/\sin K\Lambda$:

$$
M^N = \begin{pmatrix} A\,U_{N-1} - U_{N-2} & B\,U_{N-1} \\ C\,U_{N-1} & D\,U_{N-1} - U_{N-2} \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
R_N = \frac{|C|^2\,|U_{N-1}|^2}{|C|^2\,|U_{N-1}|^2 + 1} ,
$$

with $A, B, C, D$ the elements of the single-period matrix. Outside the band $K\Lambda$ is real, $U_{N-1}$ oscillates,
and the reflectance has $N - 1$ zeros between two bands, one fewer than the number of periods, which is the count the
classic card below invites. Inside the band $U_{N-1}$ grows like $\sinh(N|\mathrm{Im}\,K|\Lambda)$, and $R_N \to 1$
exponentially in $N$, in agreement with the admittance result at the centre.

::: example bragg-mirror

Outside the band the stack is nearly transparent, with ripples, one fewer minimum between bands than there are
periods. Yeh, Yariv and Hong's 1977 paper treats the periodic stack as a one-dimensional crystal: the eigenvalues
of the unit cell's transfer matrix give the Bloch wavenumber, real in the pass bands and complex in the stop bands,
and the band edges, the number of zeros and the closing of the TM gap at the Brewster angle all follow from one
dispersion relation.

::: classic yeh-1977

## Penetration depth and the phase of a mirror

A Bragg mirror does not reflect at its surface. The field decays into the stack over a few periods, and a cavity
closed by such a mirror is effectively longer than its spacer by the **penetration depth**, which for a quarter-wave
stack of small contrast is (Babic and Corzine 1992)

$$
L_\mathrm{pen} \approx \frac{\lambda_0}{4\,(n_H - n_L)} ,
$$

about 180 nm for TiO₂/SiO₂ at 600 nm and 0.4 µm for GaAs/AlAs at 1 µm. The same quantity sets how fast the mirror's
reflection phase changes with wavelength, which decides the free spectral range and the mode spacing of a VCSEL or
of a dielectric [Fabry–Pérot cavity](learn/films/bandpass-filters.html), and it is the reason a cavity between two
Bragg mirrors resonates at a wavelength slightly off the naive $2nd = m\lambda$.

## Higher bands, and the bands that vanish

The dispersion relation is periodic in $\delta$: the stop band repeats wherever the layers are an odd number of
quarter waves thick, at $\lambda_0/3$, $\lambda_0/5$, …, with the same width in $g$ (so narrower in wavelength). At
$\lambda_0/2$, where both layers are half waves, $\cos K\Lambda = 1$ exactly: the second-order band of a quarter-wave
stack has **zero width**, and the stack is transparent there. In general the $m$-th band of a stack with optical-thickness
ratio $n_H d_H : n_L d_L$ vanishes when $m\,n_H d_H/(n_H d_H + n_L d_L)$ is an integer, a selection rule that is used to suppress unwanted
bands and, run backwards, to measure a stack's thickness ratio from which bands are missing.

## At oblique incidence

Tilting the beam shortens every layer's phase thickness, $\delta_j = k_0 n_j d_j\cos\theta_j$, so the band moves to
shorter wavelengths (a Bragg mirror seen at an angle turns bluer), and splits by polarization: the admittances
$\eta_H/\eta_L$ of the two polarizations diverge, so the s band widens and the p band narrows, closing entirely at
the Brewster angle of the H/L interface, $\tan\theta_B = n_L/n_H$ inside the stack, where successive interfaces no
longer reflect p light at all. In a stack lit from air the internal angle can never reach that Brewster angle if

$$
n_0 < \frac{n_H\, n_L}{\sqrt{n_H^2 + n_L^2}} ,
$$

and with enough contrast the stop bands of all angles and both polarizations then overlap over a common range:
Fink, Winn and co-workers (1998) built such an **omnidirectional reflector** from nine pairs of polystyrene and
tellurium, a dielectric mirror for every angle. The classic card's Yeh stack, lit from inside GaAs, does reach the
Brewster angle, which is where its TM gap closes.

records.title: Fabry–Pérot etalons: a spacer between two mirrors
records.summary: A transparent spacer between two partial mirrors transmits a comb of narrow peaks: the Airy function derived from the multiple reflections, the resonance condition with the mirrors' phases, free spectral range, finesse and resolving power, what absorption in the mirrors costs, angle tuning and the Jacquinot advantage, the photon lifetime and Q of the cavity, and the Gires–Tournois phase.

references.cite: M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §7.6
H. A. Macleod, Thin-Film Optical Filters, 3rd ed. (Institute of Physics Publishing, 2001), ch. 7
G. Hernandez, Fabry–Perot Interferometers (Cambridge University Press, 1986)
J. M. Vaughan, The Fabry–Perot Interferometer (Adam Hilger, 1989)
F. Gires and P. Tournois, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 258, 6112 (1964)

records.body:
Put a transparent layer between two partially reflecting mirrors and light bounces back and forth inside it. Where
the round trip adds a whole number of wavelengths, every pass adds in phase and the cavity transmits strongly, even
though each mirror alone reflects most of the light. Elsewhere the passes cancel and the cavity reflects. Fabry and
Pérot built it in 1897 as a spectroscope; it is the resonator of every laser, the spacer of every narrowband
[filter](learn/films/bandpass-filters.html), and the simplest case in which the multiple-reflection sum can be done
by hand.

## The Airy function

Let the two mirrors have amplitude coefficients $r_1, t_1$ and $r_2, t_2$ seen from inside the spacer, and let the
round-trip phase be $\delta = \frac{4\pi}{\lambda} n d\cos\theta$. The transmitted amplitude is the sum over the
number of round trips, a geometric series,

$$
t = t_1 t_2\, e^{i\delta/2}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(r_1 r_2\, e^{i\delta}\right)^m
= \frac{t_1 t_2\, e^{i\delta/2}}{1 - r_1 r_2\, e^{i\delta}} ,
$$

which is exactly what the [transfer matrix](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html) returns for one layer, now with its
multiple-beam origin visible. With equal lossless mirrors of reflectance $R = |r|^2$ the transmittance is the
**Airy function**

$$
T(\delta) = \frac{1}{1 + F\sin^2(\delta/2 + \phi)}, \qquad F = \frac{4R}{(1 - R)^2},
$$

where $\phi$ collects the mirrors' reflection phases. $F$ is the coefficient of finesse; for $R = 0.9$ it is 360, and
the peaks, of unit height, are separated by valleys of depth $1/(1 + F)$. The Verification page's first film row
compares the engine with this formula for a plain slab.

## The resonance condition

For a spacer of index $n$ and thickness $d$ transmission peaks where the total round-trip phase is a multiple of $2\pi$,

$$
2 n d \cos\theta = \left(m - \frac{\phi_1 + \phi_2}{2\pi}\right)\lambda_m , \qquad m = 1, 2, \dots
$$

For dielectric mirrors at their design wavelength the reflection phases are 0 or $\pi$, and the condition reduces
to the spacer being a whole number of half waves. For metal mirrors they are neither: silver's reflection phase in
the visible is around $-150°$ from the glass side, so every order sits a fraction of a free spectral range away from
the half-wave position and the spacer that resonates at a given wavelength is thinner than $m\lambda/2n$. Dielectric
mirrors have the complementary subtlety: their phase varies with wavelength as if the cavity were longer by the
[penetration depth](learn/films/bragg-mirrors.html) of the mirror, which shifts the mode spacing.

## Free spectral range, finesse, resolving power

Neighbouring orders are separated in wavelength by

$$
\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{FSR} \approx \frac{\lambda^2}{2 n d \cos\theta},
\qquad
\Delta\nu_\mathrm{FSR} = \frac{c}{2 n d\cos\theta} ,
$$

so a thicker cavity packs its peaks closer (a 1 mm air gap has 150 GHz between orders, a 1 cm laser cavity 15 GHz).
The width of each peak relative to that spacing is set by the mirrors alone, through the **finesse**

$$
\mathcal{F} = \frac{\pi\sqrt{R}}{1-R} = \frac{\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{FSR}}{\delta\lambda_{1/2}} ,
$$

30 for $R = 0.9$, 300 for $R = 0.99$. The resolving power of the etalon as a spectroscope is $\lambda/\delta\lambda =
m\mathcal{F}$, the order times the finesse, which is how a centimetre-thick etalon with modest mirrors resolves
hyperfine structure that a grating cannot. Real etalons fall short of $\mathcal{F}$ through the flatness of their
plates and the parallelism of the beam: a plate flat to $\lambda/N$ limits the finesse to about $N/2$, and a beam of
half-angle $\alpha$ smears $\cos\theta$ by $\alpha^2/2$.

## What absorption costs

For an ideal lossless cavity with equal mirrors the peaks reach $T = 1$ whatever $R$ is. Metal mirrors are not
lossless. If each mirror absorbs a fraction $A$ with $R + T_\mathrm{m} + A = 1$, the peak transmittance becomes

$$
T_\mathrm{peak} = \left(\frac{T_\mathrm{m}}{1 - R}\right)^2 = \left(1 - \frac{A}{1 - R}\right)^2 ,
$$

the square of the mirrors' **potential transmittance**: what matters is the absorption relative to what the mirror
lets through, not the absorption itself. A silver mirror with $R = 0.9$ and $A = 0.04$ limits the peak to 36 %; with
$R = 0.97$ and the same $A$, to 2 %. Better metal mirrors sharpen the peaks but lower them, which is the dead end that
led to all-dielectric filters.

::: example fabry-perot-etalon

The plotted peaks stay below 1 because the silver absorbs; the check below the figure confirms that what is not
reflected or transmitted is exactly what the layers absorb. Tilting the beam shortens $d\cos\theta$ and moves every
peak to shorter wavelengths, which is how an etalon is angle-tuned.

## Angle, étendue and the Jacquinot advantage

Since $\delta$ depends on $\cos\theta$, an etalon lit by a cone of light transmits each wavelength in a ring of
angles: the **Haidinger fringes** seen through a plate held to the eye, and the reason an etalon spectrometer records
a ring pattern. For a small tilt the peak shifts by

$$
\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} \approx -\frac{\theta_0^2}{2 n^2} ,
$$

always to shorter wavelengths, and it is this dependence on $\theta^2$ rather than $\theta$ that gives the etalon its
large throughput for a given resolution, the Jacquinot advantage over a slit instrument. The same formula says how far
a tilted [bandpass filter](learn/films/bandpass-filters.html) moves, and why a filter in a converging beam broadens.

## The cavity as a resonator: lifetime and Q

Seen in time rather than frequency, a photon in the cavity survives on average
$\tau = \frac{n d}{c\,(1 - R)}$ round trips' worth of time (for $R$ close to 1), and the quality factor
$Q = \omega\tau = m\mathcal{F}$ is again the order times the finesse. A 1 mm cavity with $R = 0.99$ stores light for
about a nanosecond. The field inside at resonance is enhanced by $1/(1 - R)$ in intensity over the incident wave, which
is what a dye molecule or a nonlinear crystal placed in the spacer sees, and why cavity enhancement is a tool of
spectroscopy and of frequency conversion.

## The Gires–Tournois etalon

Make the back mirror perfect. Nothing is transmitted, $|r| = 1$ at every wavelength, and all the physics is in the
phase of the reflected wave, which sweeps through $2\pi$ around each resonance the more rapidly the higher the front
mirror's reflectance. Such a Gires–Tournois etalon (1964) is a pure phase element: a delay that depends on wavelength,
used to compensate dispersion in femtosecond lasers and fibre links, and the simplest demonstration that a lossless
structure can have a strongly frequency-dependent group delay with a perfectly flat reflectance.

## From etalons to filters

A Fabry–Pérot cavity is the core of almost every narrowband filter. Replacing the metal mirrors by
[quarter-wave stacks](learn/films/bragg-mirrors.html) removes the absorption and raises the reflectance at will, which
is the [all-dielectric bandpass filter](learn/films/bandpass-filters.html).

records.title: Bandpass filters: all-dielectric cavities
records.summary: A half-wave spacer between two quarter-wave mirrors passes one narrow band inside a broad stop band: the design (HL)^p 2L (LH)^p and why it transmits, Macleod's half-width formula and what each parameter does, the Lorentzian single-cavity line and the square-topped multi-cavity filter, the angle shift and the converging-beam limit, blocking, absorption and the narrowest filters, and the notch and rugate filters that do the opposite.

references.cite: H. A. Macleod, Thin-Film Optical Filters, 3rd ed. (Institute of Physics Publishing, 2001), ch. 7
P. W. Baumeister, Optical Coating Technology (SPIE Press, 2004), ch. 8
A. Thelen, Design of Optical Interference Coatings (McGraw-Hill, 1989), ch. 6
W. H. Southwell, Appl. Opt. 28, 5091 (1989)
P. W. Baumeister, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 48, 955 (1958)

records.body:
An all-dielectric bandpass filter is a [Fabry–Pérot cavity](learn/films/fabry-perot-etalons.html) built entirely
from quarter-wave layers, so that nothing absorbs and the mirrors can be as good as the period count allows. Two
[Bragg mirrors](learn/films/bragg-mirrors.html) of high- and low-index layers surround a spacer that is a whole
number of half waves thick at the design wavelength $\lambda_0$:

$$
(\mathrm{HL})^p \,(2\mathrm{L})^m\, (\mathrm{LH})^p ,
$$

where $p$ is the number of pairs per mirror and $m$ the cavity order. The notation is Macleod's: each letter a
quarter wave at $\lambda_0$, read from the incident medium to the substrate.

## Why it transmits

At $\lambda_0$ the spacer is a half-wave layer, which is *absent* in the transfer-matrix sense
($M = -I$). What is left is $(\mathrm{HL})^p(\mathrm{LH})^p$: the two mirrors face each other, and because the
sequence is symmetric the admittance that the second mirror builds up from the substrate is exactly undone by the
first, layer by layer, back to the substrate's own admittance $n_s$. The whole filter at $\lambda_0$ is therefore
optically the bare substrate, with $R = \left(\frac{n_0 - n_s}{n_0 + n_s}\right)^2$, 4 % for glass, and $T \approx 96 \%$
(a single antireflecting layer on the back or an absentee-corrected design removes the rest). A little away from
$\lambda_0$ the spacer is no longer absent, the mirrors are not undone, and since each reflects nearly everything the
transmittance collapses: a line, inside a stop band.

## What sets the width

The single-cavity line has the Airy shape of the etalon, which near its peak is a Lorentzian whose half-width Macleod
derives in closed form. For a spacer of low index with $p$ pairs on each side and a substrate $n_s$,

$$
\frac{\Delta\lambda_{1/2}}{\lambda_0} \approx \frac{4\,n_L^{\,2p-1}\, n_s}{m\,\pi\, n_H^{\,2p}} ,
$$

and with a high-index spacer the roles of $n_H$ and $n_L$ in the prefactor exchange. Every design knob is visible in
it:

- each extra pair on both mirrors multiplies the width by $(n_L/n_H)^2$, 0.4 for TiO₂/SiO₂: the width falls
  geometrically with $p$, as the mirrors' $1 - R$ does;
- the cavity order $m$ narrows the line in proportion, because the phase in a thicker spacer changes faster with
  wavelength; second- and third-order spacers are the usual compromise between narrowness and the tolerances of
  thicker layers;
- a high-index spacer is narrower than a low-index one with the same mirrors by $(n_H/n_L)^2$, and also shifts less
  with angle (below).

A $p = 4$, $m = 1$ TiO₂/SiO₂ filter has a half-width of about 1 % of $\lambda_0$, 5.5 nm at 550 nm; $p = 6$ gives
0.9 nm. The rejection outside the passband is the mirrors' own [stop band](learn/films/bragg-mirrors.html): its width
comes from the index contrast, so TiO₂/SiO₂ blocks about 490–630 nm around a 550 nm design, and a practical filter
adds absorbing glass or further stacks as broadband blockers beyond that, where the mirrors are transparent again.

::: example bandpass-filter

Moving the spacer away from a half wave shifts the passband through the stop band; it disappears into the edge once
the cavity's resonance leaves the band. Absorption in the layers, ignored in the ideal design, is what limits the peak
transmittance of very narrow filters: by the potential-transmittance argument of the
[etalon section](learn/films/fabry-perot-etalons.html), what counts is the absorption per pass relative to $1 - R$,
and a filter of 0.5 nm width with layers that absorb $10^{-4}$ per pass already loses a tenth of its peak.

## Multiple cavities: a square top

A single cavity has a Lorentzian line: sharp at the top but with slowly falling wings, so that a 1 nm filter still
passes a thousandth of the light 10 nm away. Putting two or three cavities in series, coupled through a shared
quarter-wave layer, $(\mathrm{HL})^p 2\mathrm{L} (\mathrm{LH})^p\, \mathrm{L}\, (\mathrm{HL})^p 2\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{LH})^p$,
splits the resonance into as many coupled modes, which together make a flat top and steep sides; the shape is the
optical analogue of a Butterworth or Chebyshev electrical filter, and the design rules carry over (Baumeister 1958).
Nearly every commercial narrowband filter is a two- or three-cavity design, and the wavelength-division multiplexers
of optical fibre links use up to a hundred cavities' worth of layers to pass one 0.4 nm channel and reject its
neighbours by $10^{-4}$.

## Angle: tuning and the converging-beam limit

Tilting the filter moves its passband to shorter wavelengths, as every interference feature moves, by

$$
\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda_0} \approx -\frac{\sin^2\theta_0}{2\,n_\mathrm{eff}^2} ,
$$

where $n_\mathrm{eff}$ is an effective index close to the spacer's (slightly modified by the mirrors). A few degrees
of tilt is the standard way to fine-tune a filter after it has been made; it also means that a filter in a cone of
half-angle $\alpha$ passes a band broadened by the same formula with $\theta_0 \to \alpha$, so a 1 nm filter in an
f/2 beam no longer has a 1 nm band. High-index spacers, with their larger $n_\mathrm{eff}$, are preferred where the beam
cannot be collimated, and a filter's data sheet always states the cone angle its curve was measured in.

## The notch filter

Swap the roles and a stack rejects one band while passing the rest. A quarter-wave mirror with very weak index
contrast (two materials differing by a few hundredths, or a mixture graded between them) has a stop band whose width,
by the Bragg formula $\Delta g = \frac{4}{\pi}\arcsin\frac{n_H - n_L}{n_H + n_L}$, is as narrow as one likes, and needs
correspondingly many periods to reach high reflectance. Southwell's **rugate** filters (1989) replace the discrete
layers by a sinusoidal index profile, whose single Fourier component produces one stop band with no higher-order
bands and no ripple; the laser-line blocking filters of Raman spectroscopy, which must reject the excitation by
$10^{-6}$ a few nanometres from a band they transmit, are built this way.

records.title: Thin metal films: beam splitters
records.summary: A few nanometres of silver divide a beam into reflected and transmitted halves: the Drude metal and the skin depth, why a metal film is partly transparent, the absorption that no design removes and Macleod's potential transmittance that bounds it, the induced-transmission trick of dielectric matching layers, the polarizing and phase-shifting behaviour at 45°, and what dielectric splitters trade for their losslessness.

P. H. Berning and A. F. Turner, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 47, 230 (1957)
P. B. Johnson and R. W. Christy, Phys. Rev. B 6, 4370 (1972)
M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), ch. 14
N. W. Ashcroft and N. D. Mermin, Solid State Physics (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1976), ch. 1

records.body:
A metal's index is mostly imaginary: silver at 550 nm has $\tilde n \approx 0.06 + 3.6i$ (Johnson and Christy 1972),
so $\varepsilon = \tilde n^2 \approx -13 + 0.4i$. The negative real part is the signature of free electrons, and it is
what makes the metal reflect; the small imaginary part is what makes it absorb. Both come out of the simplest model
of a conductor, and both are needed to understand why a film of silver can be a beam splitter at all.

## The Drude metal and the skin depth

Free electrons of density $N$ and effective mass $m$ driven by a field $E e^{-i\omega t}$ and damped at a rate
$\gamma$ give the Drude permittivity

$$
\varepsilon(\omega) = \varepsilon_\infty - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2 + i\gamma\omega},
\qquad
\omega_p^2 = \frac{N e^2}{\varepsilon_0 m} ,
$$

with the plasma frequency $\omega_p$ in the ultraviolet for the noble metals ($\hbar\omega_p \approx 9$ eV for
silver) and $\gamma \ll \omega$ in the visible. Below $\omega_p$ the real part is large and negative: the electrons
respond out of phase, screen the field, and the wave cannot propagate. Instead it decays over the **skin depth**

$$
\delta = \frac{\lambda}{4\pi k} ,
$$

12 nm in intensity for silver in the visible ($k \approx 3.6$), 25 nm for aluminium's lower $k$ in the near
ultraviolet. The interband transitions of the bound electrons (the $d$ bands) add to $\varepsilon_\infty$ and give
silver its edge near 320 nm and gold its colour; the tabulated $n, k$ contain all of it, and the Drude form is the
reason for their shape rather than a substitute for them. A film much thicker than $\delta$ is a mirror; a film
comparable to it lets a useful fraction through. That is the whole design freedom of a metallic beam splitter: one
thickness trades reflection against transmission.

## Absorption is unavoidable, and how much is bounded

In a metal, the field that does get through drives currents that dissipate. However the film is chosen,

$$
R + T + A = 1 , \qquad A > 0 ,
$$

and a 50/50 silver splitter loses a few percent to absorption, more toward the blue, where silver's $k$ falls and
its $n$ rises. Macleod's **potential transmittance** says how much a given metal layer *can* transmit if the
dielectrics around it were chosen perfectly:

$$
\psi = \frac{T}{1 - R} ,
$$

the transmittance per unit of light that enters the film. It depends on the metal layer and on the admittance
presented to its exit face, not on what is in front of it, and it has a maximum over that exit admittance. For a
given thickness of silver the maximum $\psi$ is the best any coating can do; design is then the choice of layers
that realise it (Berning and Turner 1957). This is the principle of **induced transmission**: a 30 nm silver film
alone transmits a few percent in the visible, but between two matching dielectric layers it transmits 60 % over a
band, with the rest reflected rather than absorbed. The [low-emissivity coating](learn/films/low-emissivity-coatings.html)
is this idea applied to a window.

::: example metal-beam-splitter

## s and p at 45°

At oblique incidence the two polarizations see different tilted admittances, $n\cos\theta$ for s and $n/\cos\theta$
for p (see [the transfer matrix](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html)), and a metal film therefore reflects s more
strongly than p: at 45° a 50/50 silver splitter is typically 55/45 for s and 45/55 for p, mildly polarizing. Worse
for interferometers, the two polarizations also pick up **different phases** on reflection and transmission, so a
linearly polarized beam at 45° to the plane of incidence leaves slightly elliptical. Where that matters, in
interferometers that recombine the two beams or in polarization-sensitive imaging, a compensating plate, a
polarization-insensitive multilayer or a cube splitter with the film at a lower angle is used. The same difference
is the reason the s-polarized dip of a [surface-plasmon sensor](learn/films/surface-plasmon-resonance.html) is
absent while the p-polarized one is deep.

## Dielectric splitters

A quarter-wave stack of a few periods splits a beam with no absorption at all, at the price of a narrower band and a
stronger dependence on angle and polarization: its reflectance follows the [Bragg](learn/films/bragg-mirrors.html)
curve, 50 % only near one wavelength per design, and its s and p reflectances separate faster with angle than a
metal's. Broadband dielectric splitters are therefore non-quarter-wave designs with many layers, optimised
numerically, and for the wide band and modest accuracy of a visual instrument a metal film remains the simpler and
cheaper part. Hybrid designs, a metal layer with dielectric enhancement on one side, sit between the two.

## Measuring a metal film

The optical constants of a thin metal film are not those of the bulk: a film thinner than the electron mean free
path (about 50 nm for silver) scatters its electrons at the surfaces, which raises $\gamma$ and the absorption, and
below about 10 nm an evaporated film is not continuous but an island structure with its own plasmon resonance. The
databases' $n, k$ are for thick, well-annealed films; a 10 nm beam splitter is measured, by ellipsometry or by $R$
and $T$ together, and the fitted thickness and index are what a design should use. The calculator's uploaded-table
inputs exist for exactly this case.

records.title: Low-emissivity glazing: dielectric / silver / dielectric
records.summary: An ultrathin silver film between two dielectric layers lets daylight through and reflects heat: the Drude metal below its plasma frequency, the induced-transmission design that antireflects the silver in the visible, Kirchhoff's law and the Hagen–Rubens emissivity of a conductor, the sheet-resistance rule of thumb, the glazing figures of merit, and why double- and triple-silver stacks steepen the edge.

references.cite: R. J. Martín-Palma et al., Sol. Energy Mater. Sol. Cells 53, 55 (1998)
H. A. Macleod, Thin-Film Optical Filters, 3rd ed. (Institute of Physics Publishing, 2001), ch. 7 and 9
C. G. Granqvist, Appl. Phys. A 52, 83 (1991)
E. Hagen and H. Rubens, Ann. Phys. 316, 873 (1903)
Ciesielski et al. (2017), silver n,k to 20.9 µm, refractiveindex.info main/Ag/nk/Ciesielski.yml

records.body:
A window should let daylight in and keep heat where it is. The two wavelength ranges are well separated: sunlight
carries its energy between 0.3 and 2.5 µm, the thermal radiation of a room at 20 °C peaks near 10 µm. Silver does
both jobs, if it is thin enough and dressed in the right dielectrics, and the physics is the same Drude response as
in the [beam-splitter section](learn/films/beam-splitters.html), read at two very different frequencies.

## A metal at two frequencies

Below the plasma frequency a Drude metal has $\varepsilon \approx -\omega_p^2/\omega^2$: at 550 nm silver's
$|\varepsilon|$ is about 13, at 10 µm it is about $4\,000$ with an imaginary part of similar size. The reflectance of
the bulk metal is 97 % in the visible and 99.5 % in the thermal infrared, and the skin depth shrinks from 12 nm to a
few nanometres. A film of 10–15 nm is therefore thin compared with the visible skin depth, so much of the visible
leaks through, yet is already optically thick in the infrared, where it reflects as if it were bulk. That asymmetry
is the whole principle; the dielectric layers only tidy up the visible.

## Antireflecting a metal: induced transmission

Bare, a 12 nm silver film on glass still reflects about half of the visible, because its admittance (large and
imaginary) is far from that of glass or air. Two dielectric layers of index around 2 (ZnO, TiO₂, SnO₂, Si₃N₄) on
either side act as an **induced-transmission filter** (Macleod ch. 7): each is roughly a quarter wave at the design
wavelength, and the pair rotates the stack's admittance locus so that the silver, seen from the glass, is matched to
the air. Reflections from the stack then cancel across the visible, and transmittance rises from about 50 % to 80 %,
with the remainder absorbed rather than reflected. The potential transmittance of a 12 nm silver film in the
visible, the most any matching layers can extract, is about 85 %, and commercial coatings get within a few percent of
it. In the infrared the silver's admittance is far too large for any dielectric of index 2 to match, the quarter-wave
layers are a few hundredths of a wave thick anyway, and the stack reflects as bare silver would.

## Emissivity is absorptance

By Kirchhoff's law a surface's spectral emissivity equals its spectral absorptance at the same wavelength and
direction. For an opaque coated pane $T \approx 0$ in the thermal infrared, so

$$
\varepsilon(\lambda) = A(\lambda) = 1 - R(\lambda) ,
$$

and the quantity glazing engineers quote, the **hemispherical emissivity**, is this absorptance averaged over the
room-temperature black-body spectrum and over angle. Bare glass, which absorbs strongly through its Si–O vibrations
across the whole window, has $\varepsilon \approx 0.84$; a single-silver low-e coating has 0.04–0.10, a triple-silver
stack about 0.02. A pane that emits a twentieth of what bare glass does loses a correspondingly smaller share of a
room's heat by radiation, which is about half of the loss through a window in winter.

For a good conductor the emissivity has a closed form. Hagen and Rubens (1903) showed that far below the plasma
frequency, where $\varepsilon \approx i\sigma/(\varepsilon_0\omega)$ with $\sigma$ the dc conductivity, the normal
emissivity of a thick metal is

$$
\varepsilon_\mathrm{n} \approx 2\sqrt{\frac{2\,\varepsilon_0\,\omega}{\sigma}} ,
$$

about 0.01 for silver at 10 µm, falling as $\sqrt{\omega}$ toward longer wavelengths. For a thin film the same physics
is expressed through its **sheet resistance** $R_\square = 1/(\sigma d)$: a film on a transparent substrate has, to a
good approximation, $\varepsilon \approx 4 R_\square / Z_0$ with $Z_0 = 377\,\Omega$ the impedance of free space, that
is about 0.01 per ohm per square. A 12 nm silver film has $R_\square \approx 3\,\Omega/\square$ and an emissivity near
0.03, and the rule explains at a glance why emissivity and electrical conductivity go together, why a thicker film
is always a better emitter-suppressor, and why transparent conductive oxides (ITO at 20–30 Ω/□) make hard-coat low-e
glass of emissivity 0.15–0.2 but can never reach silver's.

::: example low-e-coating

Thicker silver raises the infrared reflectance and lowers the visible transmittance; the trade-off is the one
number a glazing designer chooses. The silver data here extend to 20 µm (Ciesielski et al., 2017); the classic study
of this design is Martín-Palma et al. (1998), and Granqvist's review (1991) is the standard account of spectrally
selective coatings.

## Figures of merit, and the edge

Three numbers describe a glazing: the visible transmittance $T_\mathrm{vis}$ (weighted by the eye's sensitivity), the
solar transmittance or solar heat gain coefficient $g$ (weighted by the solar spectrum, including the fraction of
absorbed heat re-emitted inward), and the emissivity. A winter window wants high $g$ and low $\varepsilon$; a summer
window in a hot climate wants low $g$ with high $T_\mathrm{vis}$, that is a sharp cut-off at the end of the visible, near
700 nm, with the near infrared of sunlight (half its energy) reflected. The selectivity $T_\mathrm{vis}/g$ of a single
silver film is limited, because its transmittance falls off gently through the near infrared. Repeating the
dielectric/silver/dielectric unit two or three times makes the stack an induced-transmission filter with two or
three coupled cavities, which, exactly as for the [multi-cavity bandpass filter](learn/films/bandpass-filters.html),
squares the top and steepens the edge: triple-silver coatings reach $T_\mathrm{vis}/g \approx 2$, close to the
theoretical limit for the solar spectrum. The price is a lower $T_\mathrm{vis}$ and a slight colour, and the design
problem is to keep the reflected colour neutral, which the dielectric thicknesses control.

records.title: Surface plasmon resonance: the Kretschmann geometry
records.summary: A thin gold film on a prism couples p-polarized light to the surface plasmon at the gold/analyte boundary: the plasmon as a pole of the Fresnel coefficient, its dispersion relation and decay lengths, prism coupling in the Kretschmann and Otto geometries, the Lorentzian dip and critical coupling, why only p light couples, the sensitivity and figure of merit of an SPR sensor, and the limits of the model.

references.cite: E. Kretschmann and H. Raether, Z. Naturforsch. A 23, 2135 (1968)
H. Raether, Surface Plasmons on Smooth and Rough Surfaces and on Gratings (Springer, 1988), ch. 2
J. Homola, S. S. Yee and G. Gauglitz, Sens. Actuators B 54, 3 (1999)
S. A. Maier, Plasmonics: Fundamentals and Applications (Springer, 2007), ch. 2–3
P. B. Johnson and R. W. Christy, Phys. Rev. B 6, 4370 (1972)

records.body:
A surface plasmon is a charge-density wave bound to the boundary between a metal (permittivity $\varepsilon_m$, with
$\mathrm{Re}\,\varepsilon_m < 0$) and a dielectric $\varepsilon_d$. It is also, and this is the useful way to think of
it in a thin-film calculation, a **pole of the Fresnel coefficient** $r_p$ of that boundary: a wave that exists with
no incident field at all.

## The plasmon as a pole

Write $r_p$ of the metal/dielectric interface in terms of the normal wavenumbers $k_{z,d} = \sqrt{\varepsilon_d k_0^2 - k_x^2}$
and $k_{z,m} = \sqrt{\varepsilon_m k_0^2 - k_x^2}$:

$$
r_p = \frac{\varepsilon_m k_{z,d} - \varepsilon_d k_{z,m}}{\varepsilon_m k_{z,d} + \varepsilon_d k_{z,m}} .
$$

The denominator vanishes where $\varepsilon_m/k_{z,m} = -\varepsilon_d/k_{z,d}$, which with both $k_z$ imaginary (a
field decaying on both sides) requires $\varepsilon_m$ and $\varepsilon_d$ of opposite sign, and gives the
**dispersion relation**

$$
k_\mathrm{sp} = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_m \varepsilon_d}{\varepsilon_m + \varepsilon_d}} ,
$$

a wavenumber along the boundary larger than that of light in the dielectric, $k_0\sqrt{\varepsilon_d}$, for every
$\varepsilon_m < -\varepsilon_d$. The field decays away from the boundary with $1/|k_{z,d}|$ in the dielectric and
$1/|k_{z,m}|$ in the metal: for gold at 633 nm ($\varepsilon_m \approx -11.7 + 1.2i$) against water, about 250 nm into
the water and 30 nm into the gold, so the wave lives mostly on the dielectric side and is sensitive to what is there.
The imaginary part of $\varepsilon_m$ makes $k_\mathrm{sp}$ complex; the plasmon propagates a distance
$1/(2\,\mathrm{Im}\,k_\mathrm{sp})$, some 10 µm for gold in the red, before it has dissipated. The s-polarized
coefficient $r_s$ has no such pole for non-magnetic media, which is why there is no s plasmon.

Because $k_\mathrm{sp} > k_0\sqrt{\varepsilon_d}$, light arriving from the dielectric side can never match it: a flat
metal surface in air does not glow with plasmons, and a plasmon on a flat surface does not radiate. Something has to
supply the missing momentum.

## Borrowing momentum from a prism

Kretschmann and Raether (1968) put the metal film on a prism of index $n_p > \sqrt{\varepsilon_d}$. Past the critical
angle of the prism/analyte pair the light's in-plane wavenumber $k_x = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} n_p \sin\theta$ exceeds
what the analyte supports, its field is evanescent beyond the metal and tunnels through a film a few tens of
nanometres thick, and at the angle where

$$
n_p \sin\theta_\mathrm{res} = \mathrm{Re}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_m \varepsilon_d}{\varepsilon_m + \varepsilon_d}}
$$

it couples into the plasmon on the far side. In the prism / metal / analyte three-layer formula the plasmon pole of
the metal/analyte interface sits just below the real $k_x$ axis, and the reflectance seen from the prism dips as
$k_x$ passes it. Otto's geometry (1968) keeps the prism *away* from the metal, with an air or liquid gap of a few
hundred nanometres through which the evanescent wave reaches a thick metal; it is the better choice for a bulk
metal and for infrared work, Kretschmann's for a sensor, because the analyte is on the free side of the film.

## A Lorentzian dip, and critical coupling

Near the resonance the reflectance of the three-layer system has the form (Raether)

$$
R(k_x) \approx 1 - \frac{4\,\Gamma_i\,\Gamma_\mathrm{rad}}{(k_x - k_\mathrm{sp}')^2 + (\Gamma_i + \Gamma_\mathrm{rad})^2} ,
$$

where $\Gamma_i = \mathrm{Im}\,k_\mathrm{sp}$ is the plasmon's internal (ohmic) damping and $\Gamma_\mathrm{rad}$ its
radiative damping back into the prism through the film, which falls exponentially with the film's thickness. The
dip is a Lorentzian in $k_x$ (and nearly so in angle) of width $\Gamma_i + \Gamma_\mathrm{rad}$, and its depth is
governed by the ratio of the two dampings: it reaches zero exactly when $\Gamma_\mathrm{rad} = \Gamma_i$, **critical
coupling**, where the energy leaking back out interferes destructively with the directly reflected wave. Too thick a
film and the evanescent field does not reach the plasmon ($\Gamma_\mathrm{rad} \to 0$, a shallow dip); too thin and
the plasmon leaks back into the prism faster than the metal absorbs it (a broad, shallow dip). Near 50 nm of gold at
633 nm the two balance and the dip nearly reaches zero. The finite film also shifts the dip by a fraction of a degree
from the semi-infinite condition above, by the real part of the radiative correction.

## Only p light, and what s light is good for

The plasmon's field has a component normal to the surface, which is what the surface charge needs; s-polarized
light has none, so it is reflected almost totally at every angle beyond the critical one, less only the gold's weak
absorption. This makes the s reflectance a reference: the ratio $R_p/R_s$ removes the source's intensity drift and
is what most instruments record.

::: example kretschmann-spr

## A sensor

The resonance angle depends on $\varepsilon_d$, the analyte's index right at the gold surface, within the plasmon's
decay length. Molecules binding to the gold change that index by a tiny amount and shift the dip; following the dip
in real time is how SPR biosensors measure binding kinetics without labels (Homola, Yee and Gauglitz 1999). The
sensitivity follows from the dispersion relation: differentiating the resonance condition,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_\mathrm{res}}{\mathrm{d}n_d} = \frac{\varepsilon_m^{3/2}}{n_p\cos\theta_\mathrm{res}\,(\varepsilon_m + n_d^2)^{3/2}}
\;\;\text{(real parts)},
$$

about 100° per refractive-index unit for gold on a BK7 prism in water, so a change of $10^{-6}$ in index, the
resolution of a good instrument, is a millidegree. Since the dip's width is set by $\Gamma_i + \Gamma_\mathrm{rad}$, the
**figure of merit** is sensitivity over width, which favours silver (sharper, but it corrodes) over gold, longer
wavelengths (where $|\varepsilon_m|$ is larger and the plasmon lives longer), and a film at critical coupling. A
thin adhesion layer of chromium or titanium under the gold, a few nanometres, broadens the dip noticeably and is
one of the first things a film calculation shows.

## Limits of the model

The calculation assumes a flat, continuous, local metal with bulk optical constants. A rough film scatters the
plasmon into light (Raether's book is largely about this), a granular film below 20 nm has island plasmons of its
own, and the constants of an evaporated gold film differ from the bulk by a few percent, which moves the resonance
by a fraction of a degree, more than a sensor's resolution. In a measurement all of these are absorbed into a fitted
$\varepsilon_m$ and thickness, which the transfer matrix then reproduces exactly; the model's remaining limit is the
analyte layer itself, a few nanometres of protein whose index and thickness are not separately measurable from a
single angular scan, which is why two wavelengths, or an angular and a spectral scan, are used when both are wanted.

records.title: Graded index: moth-eye antireflection
records.summary: A sub-wavelength taper removes the index step instead of cancelling its reflection: the effective-medium picture and where it holds, Maxwell Garnett and Bruggeman mixing rules, the WKB view of a graded profile as the Fourier transform of its index gradient, why height matters more than shape and why smoothness matters at all, Southwell's quintic, and what the moth's eye adds that a graded film cannot.

references.cite: P. B. Clapham and M. C. Hutley, Nature 244, 281 (1973)
W. H. Southwell, Opt. Lett. 8, 584 (1983)
D. A. G. Bruggeman, Ann. Phys. 416, 636 (1935)
J. C. Maxwell Garnett, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 203, 385 (1904)
Lord Rayleigh, Proc. London Math. Soc. 11, 51 (1880)
D. G. Stavenga, S. Foletti, G. Palasantzas and K. Arikawa, Proc. R. Soc. B 273, 661 (2006)

records.body:
A [quarter-wave coating](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html) cancels one reflection at one wavelength. A gradual change
of index does something different: with no step left, there is nothing to reflect from, over a broad band and a wide
range of angles. Rayleigh showed in 1880 that a sufficiently slow transition between two media reflects nothing;
moth eyes do it with arrays of cones a few hundred nanometres tall (Clapham and Hutley 1973), and the same idea, as
graded porous films or as etched "black silicon", is the broadband antireflection of choice wherever a hard coating
is not required.

## The effective medium, and where it holds

While the period $\Lambda$ of a structure is small enough that no diffraction order but the zeroth propagates in
either medium,

$$
\Lambda < \frac{\lambda}{n_s + n_0 \sin\theta_0} ,
$$

light cannot resolve the individual features and sees their average: an **effective medium**. The condition is the
[grating cutoff](learn/films/gratings.html); for cones on glass under visible light it means periods below about
250 nm, which the moth's 200 nm array satisfies. Well below the cutoff the average is a quasi-static one, a
homogenisation of the local permittivities, and there are two classical rules for it. **Maxwell Garnett** (1904)
treats one material as inclusions in a host of the other, exact for dilute spherical inclusions:

$$
\frac{\varepsilon_e - \varepsilon_h}{\varepsilon_e + 2\varepsilon_h} = f\,\frac{\varepsilon_i - \varepsilon_h}{\varepsilon_i + 2\varepsilon_h} .
$$

**Bruggeman** (1935) treats both constituents symmetrically, each embedded in the effective medium itself,

$$
f\,\frac{\varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_e}{\varepsilon_1 + 2\varepsilon_e} + (1-f)\,\frac{\varepsilon_2 - \varepsilon_e}{\varepsilon_2 + 2\varepsilon_e} = 0 ,
$$

which is the better model for an interpenetrating structure such as a tapered array near its base, and the one the
example below and the calculator's roughness finish use. For a two-dimensional array of columns the exact answer is anisotropic and
differs from both; the difference is a few hundredths in index for dielectrics, and matters more for metals, whose
effective permittivity near the percolation threshold is a subject of its own. Slice the taper into thin layers,
give each the $\varepsilon_e$ of its local fill fraction $f(z)$, and the taper becomes an ordinary graded multilayer,
which the [transfer matrix](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html) solves exactly. A few tens of slices are enough for any
profile at visible wavelengths; the example below uses sixteen, each at the Bruggeman index of its local glass fraction.

## Why a graded profile reflects so little: the WKB view

For a slowly varying index $n(z)$ the reflection coefficient can be written, to first order in the gradient, as

$$
r \approx -\int \frac{1}{2n(z)}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}n}{\mathrm{d}z}\, e^{2i\phi(z)}\,\mathrm{d}z ,
\qquad \phi(z) = k_0\int_0^{z} n(z')\,\mathrm{d}z' :
$$

the reflected wave is the **Fourier transform of the index gradient**, taken at twice the local wavenumber. Three
consequences follow directly. An abrupt step has a gradient that is a delta function, whose transform is flat: it
reflects at every wavelength. A ramp of height $h$ has a transform that falls as $1/(k_0 h)$ with side lobes, so
reflection drops once $h$ exceeds a fraction of a wavelength and then oscillates. And the faster the transform
decays, the smoother the gradient must be: a profile whose first $m$ derivatives are continuous at both ends has a
reflectance falling as $(\lambda/h)^{2(m+1)}$.

## Height first, then shape

A graded layer stops reflecting once it is thicker than about a third of the wavelength: below that, light still sees
an abrupt step and reflects much as from the bare surface. Above it, the residual reflection depends on how smoothly
the index starts and ends. A linear ramp leaves a kink at both ends, where the gradient jumps from zero to its
value, and its reflectance falls only as $(\lambda/h)^2$; Southwell's **quintic** profile (1983),

$$
n(t) = n_0 + (n_s - n_0)\,(10t^3 - 15t^4 + 6t^5), \qquad t = z/h ,
$$

has zero first and second derivatives at both ends, and its reflectance falls as $(\lambda/h)^6$, suppressing
reflection by orders of magnitude for the same height. The fill-fraction profile of the taper, not its geometric
outline, is what has to be quintic: a cone of circular cross section has $f \propto t^2$, which is too abrupt at
the tip and too steep at the base, and the best moth-eye shapes are paraboloids or the slightly flared cones nature
grows.

::: example moth-eye-taper

The slices' indices are fixed; only their thickness scales with the height, which keeps the same profile while the
taper grows. Real moth-eye structures add scattering where the period approaches the cutoff, which an effective
medium cannot describe; the [gratings](learn/films/gratings.html) section shows where that limit falls.

## Angle and bandwidth
