Because nothing is tuned to a wavelength, a graded layer is antireflecting from the ultraviolet to wherever its
height becomes a small fraction of the wavelength, and it stays so to large angles: the WKB integral only changes
its phase argument, and the reflectance of a 400 nm quintic taper on glass stays below 0.1 % to 60° for both
polarizations, where a four-layer coating is already at 2 %. The practical limits are mechanical (a porous or
structured surface is soft and collects dirt), and, for solar cells and displays, the slight haze from residual
scattering, which is the reason the effective-medium picture must be checked by a rigorous grating calculation
before a period is chosen.

## What the moth's eye really is

The corneal nipples of moths and butterflies (Stavenga et al. 2006) are paraboloids of 200–250 nm period and
similar height, which model and measurement agree reduce the reflectance of the cuticle from about 4 % to below
0.5 % across the visible, and more at grazing incidence, where a night-flying insect's eye would otherwise glint.
The same structure is now printed into polymer films for displays, and etched into silicon and glass, where the
"black silicon" of nanometre-scale needles reaches a reflectance below 0.1 % from 300 nm to 2 µm. It works as a
graded film, except at the tips and at the base, where the array is a periodic grating and the effective medium is
only the first term of the story.

records.title: Textured surfaces: pyramids and light trapping
records.summary: Upright pyramids on silicon give reflected light a second chance: the ray geometry of a facet, the product of two reflectances and what a coating on the facets adds, the oblique path inside the wafer, the Lambertian limit of 4n² from étendue and the Yablonovitch argument, how pyramids and random textures approach it, where the ray picture stops (feature size against wavelength), and why this needs ray tracing beside the transfer matrix.

references.cite: P. Campbell and M. A. Green, J. Appl. Phys. 62, 243 (1987)
E. Yablonovitch and G. D. Cody, IEEE Trans. Electron Devices 29, 300 (1982)
E. Yablonovitch, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 72, 899 (1982)
M. A. Green, Prog. Photovolt. 10, 235 (2002)
M. A. Green, Sol. Energy Mater. Sol. Cells 92, 1305 (2008) (silicon optical constants)

records.body:
Anisotropic etching of a (100) silicon wafer in hot alkali exposes the slowly etching (111) planes and leaves a field
of upright pyramids whose facets make $\alpha = 54.74°$ (the angle between (100) and (111)) with the wafer plane. The
pyramids are several micrometres across, large compared with the wavelength, so the texture does not change the
Fresnel coefficients of each facet; it changes where a reflected ray goes next, and what happens to a ray once it is
inside. Both effects are geometric, and both are why every crystalline silicon solar cell is textured.

## Two chances to enter

A vertical ray meets a facet at the local angle of incidence $\theta_1 = \alpha$. The specularly reflected ray leaves
rotated by $2\alpha$ from the vertical; for $\alpha > 45°$ it still points downward and strikes the opposite facet, at

$$
\theta_2 = |180° - 3\alpha| = 15.8° .
$$

Light escapes only if it is reflected both times, so the front-surface reflectance becomes the product

$$
R_\mathrm{eff} = R(\theta_1)\, R(\theta_2) ,
$$

and bare silicon's 35 % at 55° times 32 % at 16° gives 11 %, against 35 % for a polished wafer. Each factor is the
reflectance of the coated silicon surface at that angle, which is a film calculation: with a 75 nm silicon nitride
layer, a quarter wave at 600 nm for the facet's angle, the factors fall to a few percent each and their product well
below one percent. The coating must be designed for the facet's incidence angle, not for normal incidence, and for
the mix of s and p that the two reflections produce (the first reflection partly polarizes the light, so the second
sees a polarization-weighted average). Rays that hit near a pyramid's base can escape after one reflection, and the
fraction that does depends on the exact geometry; a hemispherical reflectance measurement of a textured wafer sums
all of this and is what the geometric model is checked against.

::: example pyramid-facet

## Trapping inside

Once in the silicon, refracted rays travel obliquely, by $\alpha - \theta_t$ from the vertical, about 41° for the
first refraction. Weakly absorbed near-infrared light (silicon's absorption length is 100 µm at 1000 nm and a
millimetre at 1100 nm, against a 150 µm wafer) reaches the back at an angle, reflects from the back contact or back
mirror, and meets the front facets beyond their critical angle of 16°, so it is reflected back in and bounces many
times before an escape cone lets it out. The path length is multiplied, and with it the absorption in the
long-wavelength tail that sets a silicon cell's current.

## The Lambertian limit: 4n²

How much can any texture achieve? Yablonovitch (1982) answered with a thermodynamic argument. A surface that
randomises the direction of light completely (a **Lambertian** surface) fills the whole solid angle inside the slab
with radiation of uniform brightness. The density of optical modes inside a medium of index $n$ is $n^2$ times that
in air, and only the modes within the escape cone, a fraction $1/n^2$ of the hemisphere's solid angle (by Snell's law
and $\sin^2\theta_c = 1/n^2$), can leave through the front. The mean path a ray travels before it escapes is
therefore enhanced by $2n^2$ relative to a single vertical pass if the back is a mirror, and by $4n^2$ once the
double pass between front and back is counted:

$$
\langle \ell \rangle = 4 n^2\, d \approx 50\, d
$$

for silicon ($n \approx 3.5$ in the near infrared). The argument is one of étendue, or equivalently of detailed
balance between the radiation inside and outside the slab, and the limit holds for any geometry that randomises
without absorbing; it is the yardstick against which every light-trapping scheme, from pyramids to nanophotonic
gratings, is measured, and in the weakly absorbing limit the absorption of a Lambertian slab is

$$
A \approx \frac{\alpha d\,\cdot 4n^2}{1 + \alpha d\,\cdot 4n^2}
$$

(Yablonovitch and Cody 1982). Pyramids come close to it: Campbell and Green (1987) traced rays through regular and
inverted pyramids and found enhancements within a factor of two of the limit, with inverted pyramids and random
"tiler's" patterns doing best, because a regular array returns some rays to their entry facet.

## Where the ray picture stops

The geometric treatment holds while the features are many wavelengths across and the surfaces between them are
locally flat. A texture of a few hundred nanometres, such as the random "black silicon" of
[the moth-eye section](learn/films/moth-eye-antireflection.html) or a periodic nanograting, is neither: it
diffracts, and its light trapping is a question of coupling into the guided modes of the wafer, which can exceed
$4n^2$ over a narrow band and falls short over a broad one. Between the two regimes, pyramids of a micrometre,
nothing simple applies and a rigorous solver is needed. Following rays through the whole wafer, with its coatings and
its back reflector, also needs **ray tracing** rather than a transfer matrix; the calculator's surface textures do it
with RayFlare, a separate engine that applies the transfer-matrix reflectances of the coated facets to each ray and
counts where it goes. The per-facet reflectance of the example above is the ingredient of that calculation, and the
check that it is right.

records.title: Gratings: diffraction orders and the sub-wavelength limit
records.summary: A periodic surface couples light into discrete orders: the grating equation from the conservation of in-plane momentum modulo 2π/Λ, propagating and evanescent orders and the cutoff, Rayleigh–Wood anomalies, the effective film a sub-wavelength grating becomes (Rytov's zeroth- and second-order indices and form birefringence), and how rigorous coupled-wave analysis solves the rest, with the Fourier factorization rules that make it converge.

references.cite: M. G. Moharam and T. K. Gaylord, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 71, 811 (1981)
M. G. Moharam, E. B. Grann, D. A. Pommet and T. K. Gaylord, J. Opt. Soc. Am. A 12, 1068 (1995)
L. Li, J. Opt. Soc. Am. A 13, 1870 (1996)
S. M. Rytov, Sov. Phys. JETP 2, 466 (1956)
D. H. Raguin and G. M. Morris, Appl. Opt. 32, 1154 (1993)
E. Popov (ed.), Gratings: Theory and Numeric Applications, 2nd ed. (Institut Fresnel, 2014)

records.body:
A planar stack conserves the in-plane wave vector exactly, because it is invariant under every translation along
the surface. A grating of period $\Lambda$ is invariant only under translations by $\Lambda$, so Bloch's theorem (the
same one that gives the [Bragg mirror](learn/films/bragg-mirrors.html) its band structure, now applied along the
surface) says the field is a sum of plane waves whose in-plane wavenumbers differ from the incident one by multiples
of $2\pi/\Lambda$. These are the diffraction orders $m$, each leaving at the angle given by the **grating equation**

$$
n \sin\theta_m = n_0 \sin\theta_0 + m\,\frac{\lambda}{\Lambda} ,
$$

in the medium of index $n$ on either side. The equation says where the orders go; it says nothing about how much
light each carries, which is the whole difficulty of grating theory.

## Propagating and evanescent orders

Order $m$ propagates in a medium of index $n$ only while $|n \sin\theta_m| < n$; beyond that its normal wavenumber is
imaginary, it is evanescent, bound to the surface, and carries no power away. As the period shrinks, or the wavelength
grows, the orders cut off one by one, the last of them ($m = -1$ into the denser medium) at

$$
\lambda_c = \Lambda\,(n_\mathrm{max} + n_0 \sin\theta_0),
$$

where $n_\mathrm{max}$ is the larger of the two media's indices. A 300 nm grating on glass at normal incidence
diffracts into the glass below 456 nm and into air below 300 nm. Exactly at a cutoff an order grazes the surface,
and the redistribution of its power among the others produces a sharp feature in every efficiency curve: the
**Rayleigh–Wood anomaly**, which Wood saw in 1902 as dark bands in a grating's spectrum and Rayleigh explained in
1907. Near a cutoff a grating is also most sensitive to its profile, which is where the simple models fail first.

## Above cutoff: an effective film

Past $\lambda_c$ only the zeroth order survives, and to it the grating is a homogeneous but **anisotropic** layer: the
field averages over the period, but it averages differently for the component along the lines and the component
across them, because the boundary conditions preserve $E_\parallel$ along the lines and $D_\perp$ across them. For a
line grating of fill fraction $f$ the lowest-order effective indices (Rytov 1956) are

$$
n_\mathrm{TE}^2 = f\,n_1^2 + (1-f)\,n_2^2, \qquad \frac{1}{n_\mathrm{TM}^2} = \frac{f}{n_1^2} + \frac{1-f}{n_2^2},
$$

the arithmetic mean of the permittivities for light polarized along the lines and the harmonic mean for light
polarized across them, the same two averages as capacitors in parallel and in series. Rytov's second-order
correction adds the first effect of the finite period,

$$
n_\mathrm{TE,2}^2 = n_\mathrm{TE}^2 + \frac{\pi^2}{3}\left(\frac{\Lambda}{\lambda}\right)^2 f^2(1-f)^2\,(n_1^2 - n_2^2)^2 ,
$$

and a corresponding term for TM, which is how far one can trust the zeroth-order picture: a few percent in index
at $\Lambda/\lambda = 0.3$ for a glass/air grating, more for silicon. The birefringence $n_\mathrm{TE} - n_\mathrm{TM}$
is a design tool in its own right, the **form birefringence** of wave plates and polarizers etched into a single
material (Raguin and Morris 1993), and for TE light the grating reflects exactly like the film below.

::: example grating-effective-film

Below the cutoff the effective film is wrong: energy leaves along the diffracted orders, which no planar calculation
produces, and the anomaly at the cutoff itself is invisible to it.

## Below cutoff: rigorous coupled-wave analysis

Gratings are solved exactly, for any period and profile, by **rigorous coupled-wave analysis** (Moharam and Gaylord
1981). The permittivity in the grating layer is expanded in its Fourier series, the field in a finite number of
Bloch harmonics (the orders, propagating and evanescent alike, $2N + 1$ of them), and Maxwell's equations in the
layer become a matrix eigenvalue problem whose eigenvectors are the layer's modes and whose eigenvalues their
propagation constants. Each mode is then an ordinary plane-wave-like solution, and the boundary conditions at the
top and bottom of the layer are a transfer-matrix problem of size $2(2N+1)$ rather than $2$: the
[Foundations](learn/common/why-transfer-matrices.html) construction, with the single channel replaced by a block of
coupled ones. A profile that is not a rectangle is staircased into slices, each with its own eigenproblem, and the
slices are joined as layers are.

Two refinements made the method practical. The products of the transfer matrices through a thick or absorbing
grating overflow exactly as they do for films, and the scattering-matrix formulation with Redheffer's star product
(the *enhanced transmittance matrix* of Moharam et al. 1995, and Li's stable algorithms) cured it. And the TM
polarization converged painfully slowly for metallic gratings until Li (1996) showed why: the product of two
discontinuous functions ($\varepsilon$ and $E_\perp$, whose product $D_\perp$ is continuous) must be Fourier
factorised by the inverse rule, $\left[\varepsilon\right]^{-1}$ of the Toeplitz matrix of $1/\varepsilon$, not by
Laurent's rule. With both, RCWA converges with a few tens of harmonics for dielectric gratings and a hundred or so
for metals, and it is what the calculator runs for its grating layers, outside PyStratify. The zero-patterning limit
of that solver reproduces the transfer matrix to $10^{-9}$, which is one of the [Verification](verification.html)
rows.

## What a grating is for

Below cutoff a grating is a spectrometer's dispersing element, a coupler into a waveguide (the $m = 1$ order matched
to a guided mode's wavenumber, the standard way light enters a photonic chip), a light-trapping structure on a solar
cell (the orders diffracted beyond the critical angle of the substrate stay inside it, as the
[textured surface](learn/films/textured-surfaces.html) does geometrically), and an anomaly-based sensor. Above cutoff
it is a film with a designable index and birefringence, the effective-medium route to the
[moth-eye antireflection](learn/films/moth-eye-antireflection.html) and to artificial wave plates. The same equation
and the same solver cover both, and the cutoff $\lambda_c$ is the line between them.

records.title: Solar cells: where the light is absorbed
records.summary: Total absorption is not what a solar cell needs: the absorbed power density from the field, the layer-resolved absorptance from the Poynting flux and its conservation check, the standing wave in a thin stack and how it moves with thickness, the photocurrent from the AM1.5 spectrum, parasitic absorption in contacts and transport layers, and the Lambertian ceiling that textures aim at.

references.cite: L. A. A. Pettersson, L. S. Roman and O. Inganäs, J. Appl. Phys. 86, 487 (1999)
G. F. Burkhard, E. T. Hoke and M. D. McGehee, Adv. Mater. 22, 3293 (2010)
P. Peumans, A. Yakimov and S. R. Forrest, J. Appl. Phys. 93, 3693 (2003)
ASTM G173-03, Standard Tables for Reference Solar Spectral Irradiances (AM1.5 global)
S. J. Byrnes, Multilayer optical calculations, arXiv:1603.02720 (2016)

records.body:
A photon makes current only if it is absorbed in the active layer. Light absorbed in the transparent electrode, the
transport layers or the metal contact is heat. A thin-film cell is therefore designed not for maximum absorption but
for maximum absorption *in one layer*, and that needs the absorptance of every layer separately, which the transfer
matrix provides from the fields it already computes. Pettersson, Roman and Inganäs (1999) wrote this out for organic
cells, Peumans and Forrest and then Burkhard, Hoke and McGehee turned it into the standard optical model of thin-film
photovoltaics, and the same calculation serves perovskite, CIGS and thin silicon cells alike.

## The absorbed power density

In an absorbing layer of complex index $\tilde n = n + ik$ the time-averaged power dissipated per unit volume is

$$
q(z) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\omega\,\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{Im}\,\varepsilon\,|E(z)|^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\omega\,\varepsilon_0\, 2nk\,|E(z)|^2 ,
$$

proportional to the local intensity, with the absorption coefficient $\alpha = 4\pi k/\lambda$ hidden in $2nk$. The
field $E(z)$ in a layer is the sum of the forward and backward amplitudes the
[transfer matrix](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html) returns, $a\,e^{ik_z z} + b\,e^{-ik_z z}$, so $|E|^2$ contains
the two decaying exponentials and their interference term, and $q(z)$ integrated over the layer is a closed form in
$a$, $b$ and $k_z$ (Pettersson's equations), which is what PyStratify evaluates. The profile $|E(z)|^2$ is the
calculator's field panel; its integral layer by layer is the per-layer absorptance.

## Absorptance from the Poynting flux

Equivalently, energy conservation in each layer says that what flows in and does not flow out is absorbed. With
$S_j^\mathrm{in}$ and $S_j^\mathrm{out}$ the normal components of the time-averaged Poynting vector at the layer's two
faces and $S_0$ the incident flux,

$$
A_j(\lambda) = \frac{S_j^\mathrm{in} - S_j^\mathrm{out}}{S_0},
\qquad
\sum_j A_j = 1 - R - T .
$$

The two routes must agree, and the sum rule is the check: PyStratify computes $A_j$ for every layer, and the check
under the example confirms that the layers' absorptances, $R$ and $T$ add to one to $10^{-9}$, Poynting's theorem
applied to the whole stack. A layer with $k = 0$ gets exactly $A_j = 0$ whatever the field inside it, which a numerical
integration of $|E|^2$ would not reproduce; the flux difference does.

::: example perovskite-cell

## The standing wave, and thickness

In a stack this thin the field inside is a standing wave: the back contact reflects nearly everything, so the
intensity has a node at the metal and antinodes a quarter wave (in the material) away from it. An absorber placed at
an antinode absorbs strongly, at a node weakly, and since the node spacing is $\lambda/2n$, a change of absorber
thickness of 50–100 nm moves the active layer from one to the other for a given wavelength. This is why the
absorption of a thin organic or perovskite cell oscillates with thickness and why its external quantum efficiency
has interference fringes rather than the smooth Beer–Lambert rise of a thick absorber. Thickening the perovskite
absorbs more of the red, up to the point where the light is gone before it reaches the back contact; beyond that
the extra thickness only adds collection losses, and the optimum is found by the photocurrent, not by the
absorptance at one wavelength.

## The photocurrent

Weighting $A_\mathrm{active}(\lambda)$ by the solar photon flux gives the current a perfect collector would deliver:

$$
J_\mathrm{sc}^\mathrm{max} = q\int A_\mathrm{active}(\lambda)\,\Phi_\mathrm{AM1.5}(\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda ,
$$

with $\Phi$ the AM1.5 global photon flux (ASTM G173; about $4.4 \times 10^{21}$ photons m⁻² s⁻¹ below 1100 nm,
corresponding to 44 mA cm⁻² if every one were absorbed in silicon). This is the figure of merit the optical models of
organic and perovskite cells optimise (Burkhard, Hoke and McGehee 2010), layer thickness by layer thickness, and the
one the calculator's sweeps are for. A measured external quantum efficiency divided by the computed $A_\mathrm{active}$
is the internal quantum efficiency, the electrical part of the problem separated from the optical one, which is the
main practical use of the layer-resolved calculation: it tells whether a cell loses photons or carriers.

## Parasitic absorption

Every other layer's $A_j$ is a loss, and the model tells which. Indium tin oxide absorbs in the blue (its band edge)
and in the near infrared (its free electrons; the trade-off with sheet resistance of the
[low-emissivity section](learn/films/low-emissivity-coatings.html)), typically 5–10 % of the current in a thin-film
cell; a 20 nm PEDOT:PSS or a doped transport layer a few percent; the metal back contact a few percent of the
long-wavelength light, more if the contact is rough or the stack is designed so that an antinode sits at the metal.
Silver loses less than aluminium, and a thin dielectric spacer between the absorber and the metal (which pushes the
antinode out of the metal) is the standard fix for both organic and silicon cells. The totals are what the layer
absorptances add up to, and an optical loss budget of a cell is a bar chart of them.

## Beyond a planar stack

A planar calculation assumes a single pass per reflection. Thick silicon cells trap light with
[textured surfaces](learn/films/textured-surfaces.html), whose ceiling is Yablonovitch's $4n^2$, and thin cells with
gratings and scattering back reflectors; the per-layer absorption of a textured cell comes from a ray-tracing or
grating solver fed with the planar coefficients of each facet, which is how the calculator's textured surfaces
compute it. The planar stack remains the reference case: it is exact, it is fast, and it is what the textured
result must reduce to when the texture is removed.

records.title: Radiative cooling: emitting into the sky
records.summary: A surface that reflects sunlight and emits in the 8–13 µm atmospheric window can cool below ambient: the power balance of a radiative cooler and the sky's own emission, Kirchhoff's law and emissivity from a film calculation, the phonon bands of silica and silicon nitride as Lorentz oscillators and the reststrahlen reflection they cause, the silver mirror underneath, directional emissivity, and what the ideal selective emitter looks like.

references.cite: A. P. Raman, M. A. Anoma, L. Zhu, E. Rephaeli and S. Fan, Nature 515, 540 (2014)
E. Rephaeli, A. Raman and S. Fan, Nano Lett. 13, 1457 (2013)
C. G. Granqvist and A. Hjortsberg, J. Appl. Phys. 52, 4205 (1981)
Y. Zhai et al., Science 355, 1062 (2017)
J. Kischkat et al., Appl. Opt. 51, 6789 (2012)
M. Planck, Ann. Phys. 309, 553 (1901)

records.body:
The atmosphere is nearly transparent between 8 and 13 µm, where the room-temperature black-body spectrum peaks. A
surface that emits strongly in that window radiates heat straight to the cold of space, at an effective
temperature far below any terrestrial one; if it also reflects sunlight, it cools below the ambient air even in
daylight. The physics was known to Granqvist in 1981, who cooled at night with silicon-monoxide films; Raman, Fan
and co-workers (2014) first did it under the sun, with a seven-layer stack of hafnia and silica on silver, and
polymer and glass-bead films (Zhai et al. 2017) have since made it a material rather than a device. All of it is a
question of designing one reflectance spectrum.

## The power balance

A cooler at temperature $T$ facing the sky exchanges radiation in both directions. Its net cooling power per unit
area is

$$
P_\mathrm{cool}(T) = P_\mathrm{rad}(T) - P_\mathrm{atm}(T_\mathrm{amb}) - P_\mathrm{sun} - P_\mathrm{cond+conv} ,
$$

with the radiated power an integral of Planck's spectrum $I_\mathrm{BB}(\lambda, T)$ over wavelength and over the
hemisphere, weighted by the surface's emissivity $\varepsilon(\lambda, \theta)$:

$$
P_\mathrm{rad}(T) = 2\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}\!\!\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta \int_0^\infty I_\mathrm{BB}(\lambda, T)\,\varepsilon(\lambda, \theta)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda .
$$

The atmosphere radiates back with its own emissivity $\varepsilon_\mathrm{atm}(\lambda, \theta) = 1 - t(\lambda)^{1/\cos\theta}$,
nearly black outside the window (water vapour, CO₂) and nearly transparent inside it at the zenith, less so toward
the horizon; $P_\mathrm{atm}$ is the same integral with the product of the two emissivities. The sun adds its
irradiance times the surface's solar absorptance, up to 1000 W m⁻², and conduction and convection from the air add
roughly $h\,(T_\mathrm{amb} - T)$ with $h$ of a few W m⁻² K⁻¹, which is what a wind shield is for. A black body at 300 K
radiates 460 W m⁻²; the window carries about a third of that, and a surface that emits only in the window and
nothing elsewhere, while reflecting the sun entirely, reaches a net cooling power of order 100 W m⁻² at ambient and
a temperature 10–20 K below ambient at zero load. That is the target the spectrum has to meet: $\varepsilon \approx 1$
for 8–13 µm, $\varepsilon \approx 0$ (and $R \approx 1$) for 0.3–2.5 µm and, for a sub-ambient cooler, outside the window
too, where the atmosphere is warm and would heat the surface.

## Emissivity from a film calculation

By Kirchhoff's law a surface's spectral emissivity equals its absorptance at the same wavelength and direction: a body
in equilibrium with radiation must emit what it absorbs, wavelength by wavelength and direction by direction. On an
opaque mirror nothing is transmitted, so

$$
\varepsilon(\lambda, \theta) = A(\lambda, \theta) = 1 - R(\lambda, \theta),
\qquad
\bar\varepsilon_{8\text{–}13} = \langle A \rangle_{8\text{–}13\,\mu\mathrm{m}} ,
$$

and designing an emitter is designing a reflectance spectrum: low in the window, high everywhere the sun shines. The
transfer matrix gives $A$ at every angle for both polarizations, and the hemispherical integral above is a sum over
the calculator's angle sweep weighted by $\sin\theta\cos\theta$.

## Phonon bands and a mirror

Silica and silicon nitride absorb strongly in the window through their lattice vibrations, and are transparent in
the visible. Each infrared-active vibration is a **Lorentz oscillator**,

$$
\varepsilon(\omega) = \varepsilon_\infty + \frac{\Delta\varepsilon\,\omega_\mathrm{TO}^2}{\omega_\mathrm{TO}^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega} ,
$$

whose real part is negative between the transverse-optical frequency $\omega_\mathrm{TO}$ and the longitudinal one
$\omega_\mathrm{LO}$: in that **reststrahlen band** the material behaves like a metal and *reflects* instead of
absorbing. Silica's Si–O stretch has $\omega_\mathrm{TO}$ near 1070 cm⁻¹ (9.3 µm) and a reststrahlen band from
about 8 to 9.3 µm, right in the middle of the window, where a thick silica layer reflects 70 % and emits 30 %;
silicon nitride's Si–N band lies near 11.5 µm, and the two complement each other. A thin layer of either on silver
emits near its absorption peak, while the silver, seen through the transparent layer, reflects most of the solar
spectrum; Granqvist's SiO on aluminium was the first of these. Silica alone leaves a gap in the window where it
reflects; stacking it with silicon nitride, or using several thinner layers of alternating materials (Raman's
hafnia/silica stack, which also antireflects the silver in the infrared), fills it, and the design problem is to
place the layers' thicknesses so that the window is covered while the solar reflectance stays above 97 %.

::: example radiative-cooler

The window average depends on thickness: a micron of silica begins to emit across the band, while too thick a layer
pushes the reststrahlen reflection back up. Mid-infrared constants are from Kischkat et al. (2012); silver from
Ciesielski et al. (2017), both via refractiveindex.info, and the Lorentz form above is what Kischkat fitted to
measure them.

## Direction, and the ideal emitter

The atmosphere is most transparent toward the zenith, so a cooler that emitted only into a narrow cone around the
vertical would exchange with the coldest part of the sky and reach the lowest temperature, at the price of less total
power; a near-Lambertian emitter, which most films are, gets more power and a higher floor. The directional
emissivity of a film stack is a free design variable: a thin absorbing film on a metal emits strongly near the
Brewster angle of p light and weakly at grazing incidence, which can be tuned with the layer thicknesses, and a
micro-structured surface (gratings, the photonic crystals of Rephaeli, Raman and Fan's 2013 design) can shape it
further. The ideal selective emitter for sub-ambient cooling is a step function in wavelength, unity in the window
and zero outside it, and black only where the atmosphere is clear; for cooling a hot object, such as a solar cell
or a roof, a broadband emitter is better, since every wavelength then carries heat away. Which one a given stack
approximates is read off its computed $A(\lambda)$, and the calculator's example is a two-layer start on it.

records.title: A dipole near a plane interface: emitters in thin films
records.summary: How a molecule, a quantum dot or an OLED emitter radiates when it sits in a stratified medium: the plane-wave expansion of a dipole field, the Chance–Prock–Silbey integrals for its decay rate, the channels its power goes to (escaping light, substrate modes, guided modes, absorption), quenching near a metal and the microcavity effect that OLED design is built on.

references.cite: W. Lukosz and R. E. Kunz, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 67, 1607 (1977)
R. R. Chance, A. Prock and R. Silbey, Adv. Chem. Phys. 37, 1 (1978)
G. W. Ford and W. H. Weber, Phys. Rep. 113, 195 (1984)
W. L. Barnes, J. Mod. Opt. 45, 661 (1998)
K. A. Neyts, J. Opt. Soc. Am. A 15, 962 (1998)
L. Novotny and B. Hecht, Principles of Nano-Optics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge University Press, 2012), ch. 10
M. Furno, R. Meerheim, S. Hofmann, B. Lüssem and K. Leo, Phys. Rev. B 85, 115205 (2012)

records.body:
An excited molecule is, to classical electrodynamics, an oscillating point dipole. In free space it radiates the
power $P_0$ and decays at the rate $\Gamma_0$. Put the same dipole a few hundred nanometres from a glass surface, inside
an organic layer on a mirror, or on top of a metal film, and both change: the field it radiates comes back to it,
reflected by every interface, and does work on it. This is Purcell's observation applied to a planar structure, and
it is the physics of OLED outcoupling, of surface-enhanced fluorescence and of the quenching that kills emission next
to a metal. It is computed with the same transfer matrix as a plane-wave spectrum, applied to a different source.

## A dipole as a sum of plane waves

The field of a dipole at height $z_0$ above a stack, in a medium of index $n_1$ and wavenumber $k_1 = n_1 k_0$, can be
written as a superposition of plane waves with every in-plane wavenumber $k_\parallel$, including $k_\parallel > k_1$,
for which $k_z = \sqrt{k_1^2 - k_\parallel^2}$ is imaginary and the wave is evanescent. Each plane wave meets the stack
below and returns multiplied by the stack's reflection coefficient $r^s(k_\parallel)$ or $r^p(k_\parallel)$, the
quantities the [transfer matrix](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html) already computes, now evaluated at complex angles.
Summing the reflected waves at the dipole's own position gives the reflected field there, and the work it does on the
dipole is the change in radiated power. With $s = k_\parallel / k_1$ and $s_z = \sqrt{1 - s^2}$, the result for a
dipole perpendicular and parallel to the interface is (Chance, Prock and Silbey; Lukosz and Kunz)

$$
\frac{P_\perp}{P_0} = 1 + \frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\int_0^\infty \frac{s^3}{s_z}\, r^p(s)\, e^{2 i k_1 z_0 s_z}\,\mathrm{d}s,
\qquad
\frac{P_\parallel}{P_0} = 1 + \frac{3}{4}\,\mathrm{Re}\int_0^\infty \frac{s}{s_z}\left[r^s(s) - s_z^2\, r^p(s)\right] e^{2 i k_1 z_0 s_z}\,\mathrm{d}s .
$$

An emitter with intrinsic quantum yield $q_0 < 1$ also decays non-radiatively inside itself, so its total rate is
$\Gamma/\Gamma_0 = (1 - q_0) + q_0\, P/P_0$; a randomly oriented ensemble averages one perpendicular and two parallel
dipoles. The same integrals, with the transmission coefficients in place of $r$, give the power that crosses the
stack into the substrate. Everything about the structure enters through $r^s$ and $r^p$ as functions of $s$, which
is why a dipole calculation costs little more than an angle-resolved reflectance.

## Reading the integrand: where the power goes

The integration variable $s$ sorts the dipole's power into channels, and the calculator reports them separately:

- $0 \le s < 1$: plane waves that propagate in the dipole's own medium. Part escapes (into air above an OLED, into
  the objective of a microscope); the rest is reflected and interferes with the direct wave, which makes the rate
  **oscillate with $z_0$** with a period of half a wavelength in the medium. That oscillation is Lukosz and Kunz's
  curve, and Drexhage's 1970 experiment with europium layers above a silver mirror.
- $1 \le s < n_\mathrm{sub}/n_1$: evanescent in the emitter's medium but propagating in a denser substrate: light
  that enters the glass beyond its critical angle and is **trapped in the substrate** by total internal reflection
  unless the substrate is thin or textured.
- Discrete values of $s$ at which $r^s$ or $r^p$ has a pole: the **guided modes** of the stack (and the surface
  plasmon of a metal film), which take power without radiating it. In a lossless structure these are sharp poles on
  the real axis and PyStratify integrates around them analytically, which is why its guided fraction is exact and not
  a matter of grid resolution.
- $s \gg 1$: deeply evanescent waves that reach only a few nanometres. Against an absorbing medium they deposit the
  dipole's energy directly in it. For a dipole at distance $d$ from a metal this term grows like $(k_1 d)^{-3}$, the
  quasi-static image-dipole law, with the perpendicular dipole quenched twice as strongly as the parallel one: this
  is **quenching**, and it dominates below about 10 nm.

The sum of the four channels is the total rate; the escaping part divided by the total is the outcoupling efficiency
of an OLED or the collection efficiency of a single-molecule experiment.

::: classic lukosz-kunz-1977

## The microcavity effect and OLED design

In a thin-film light-emitting diode the emitter sits in an organic layer a fraction of a wavelength thick, between a
metal cathode and a transparent anode on glass. The cathode's reflection coefficient is close to $-1$, so the
reflected wave returns with a phase set almost entirely by the round-trip distance $2 n z_0 k_0$. At the distance where
it returns in phase the dipole radiates more, mostly towards the surface normal; a quarter wave away it radiates less,
and what it radiates goes sideways into guided modes. Neyts computed the two numbers an OLED engineer needs as the
emitter moves through the layer: the fraction of power that reaches air, and the total rate $F$ (the Purcell factor),
whose product with the intrinsic quantum yield is the effective yield. Furno and co-workers turned the same integrals
into the loss budget of a complete device, with each loss channel (substrate, waveguide, surface plasmon, absorption)
against the thickness of every layer, the analysis PyStratify's film emission reproduces.

::: classic neyts-1998

Two practical rules follow from the integrals. First, the optimum emitter position is **not** at the antinode of the
plane-wave standing wave but slightly closer to the mirror, because the evanescent channels grow monotonically as the
emitter approaches it. Second, a thick transparent substrate is a trap: without outcoupling structures roughly half of
what leaves the organic layers is lost in it, which is why the [coherence and thick substrate](learn/films/coherence.html)
section's incoherent treatment matters for devices and why textured surfaces appear in the
[graded and textured surfaces](learn/films/textured-surfaces.html) chapter.

## Limits of the model

The emitter is a classical point dipole with a fixed frequency: linewidths, saturation and the modification of the
emission *spectrum* by a strongly dispersive cavity are outside it, though the rates it gives are exactly what a
quantum treatment yields for a two-level system at weak coupling. The media are local and the interfaces sharp: at
distances below one or two nanometres from a metal, the electron gas's nonlocal response and the atomic structure of
the surface change the quenching law, which is why computed rates at contact are a limit rather than a prediction. The
calculator refuses an absorbing medium *around* the emitter (its power would not be defined without a cavity around
the point source); a metal electrode is therefore an opaque layer rather than a half-space, which changes nothing in
the physics once the layer is thicker than its skin depth.

records.title: Scattering by an infinite cylinder: two polarizations
records.summary: The plane-wave solution for an infinitely long circular cylinder: cylindrical waves, the two decoupled polarizations at normal incidence and their coefficients, efficiencies per unit length, the thin-wire limit with its ε = −1 resonance, coated cylinders by the same recursion, oblique incidence, and the single-channel bound that superscattering beats.

references.cite: Lord Rayleigh, Phil. Mag. 36, 365 (1918)
C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles (Wiley, 1983), ch. 8
M. Kerker, The Scattering of Light and Other Electromagnetic Radiation (Academic Press, 1969), ch. 6
Z. Ruan and S. Fan, Phys. Rev. Lett. 105, 013901 (2010)
L. Cao et al., Nat. Mater. 8, 643 (2009)

records.body:
A cylinder is the two-dimensional cousin of a sphere, and it keeps a feature the sphere loses by symmetry: it tells the
two polarizations of the incident light apart. Rayleigh solved the problem for a dielectric cylinder at normal
incidence in 1918; Bohren and Huffman's chapter 8 is the standard modern account and the source of the notation
below. Everything on this page is for an infinitely long circular cylinder of radius $a$ in a host of index $n_h$,
lit by a plane wave of vacuum wavelength $\lambda$. The size parameter and relative index are as for a sphere,

$$
x = \frac{2\pi n_h a}{\lambda} = k a, \qquad m = \frac{n_c}{n_h}.
$$

## Cylindrical waves and the two cases

In cylindrical coordinates $(\rho, \varphi, z)$ the vector Helmholtz equation separates into modes $e^{i m\varphi}\,
e^{i k_z z}$ whose radial dependence obeys Bessel's equation (the [Foundations](learn/common/maxwell-and-boundary-conditions.html)
table). The regular solution is $J_m(q\rho)$ and the outgoing one $H^{(1)}_m(q\rho)$, with $q = \sqrt{k^2 - k_z^2}$ the
radial wavenumber. At **normal incidence**, $k_z = 0$, $q = k$, and the problem splits into two independent cases,
named after the field component along the axis:

- **Case I**: the incident electric field is parallel to the cylinder axis (TM with respect to the axis; the
  calculator's *E along the axis*). The axial component $E_z$ is the scalar field; $\mathbf{H}$ lies in the cross
  section.
- **Case II**: the incident magnetic field is parallel to the axis (TE; *H along the axis*). Now $H_z$ is the scalar,
  and $\mathbf{E}$ lies in the cross section.

For each order $m$ the two boundary conditions, continuity of the tangential $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ at
$\rho = a$, fix one scattering coefficient per case, exactly as for the [transfer matrix](learn/common/why-transfer-matrices.html)
of any stratified geometry. Bohren and Huffman's results for a non-magnetic cylinder are

$$
b_m^{\mathrm{I}} = \frac{m\,J_m(mx)\,J_m'(x) - J_m(x)\,J_m'(mx)}{m\,J_m(mx)\,H_m^{(1)\prime}(x) - H_m^{(1)}(x)\,J_m'(mx)},
\qquad
a_m^{\mathrm{II}} = \frac{J_m(mx)\,J_m'(x) - m\,J_m(x)\,J_m'(mx)}{J_m(mx)\,H_m^{(1)\prime}(x) - m\,H_m^{(1)}(x)\,J_m'(mx)},
$$

the relative index $m$ in the two expressions sitting where the sphere's $a_\ell$ and $b_\ell$ have it, swapped
between the cases. The resonances are the near-zeros of the denominators: for a dielectric they are the whispering-gallery
or **leaky modes** of the rod, which make a silicon nanowire of a given diameter absorb one colour preferentially
(Cao et al. 2009); for a metal they are the surface plasmons of the wire.

## Efficiencies per unit length

An infinite cylinder has no cross-sectional area to normalise with, so one works per unit length. The scattering
and extinction *widths* $C_\mathrm{sca}$, $C_\mathrm{ext}$ (a length) divided by the geometric width $2a$ give the
efficiencies

$$
Q_\mathrm{sca}^{\mathrm{I}} = \frac{2}{x}\left[|b_0^{\mathrm{I}}|^2 + 2\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} |b_m^{\mathrm{I}}|^2\right],
\qquad
Q_\mathrm{ext}^{\mathrm{I}} = \frac{2}{x}\,\mathrm{Re}\left[b_0^{\mathrm{I}} + 2\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} b_m^{\mathrm{I}}\right],
$$

and the same with $a_m^{\mathrm{II}}$ for case II; $Q_\mathrm{abs} = Q_\mathrm{ext} - Q_\mathrm{sca}$, and
unpolarized light averages the two cases. The orders $\pm m$ give equal contributions, hence the factor 2. The series
stops a few orders beyond $x$, as Mie's does. Bohren and Huffman plot instead the scattering per unit *volume*,
$C_\mathrm{sca}/V = 4 Q_\mathrm{sca}/(\pi d)$ with $d = 2a$, which tends to the geometric-optics asymptote $8/(\pi d)$
as $Q \to 2$: the quantity a chemist measuring turbidity cares about.

::: example glass-cylinder

The two polarizations differ most strongly at a few hundred nanometres of radius, where case I rises first and case
II lags: a resonance of case I at a given order $m$ needs the electric field to fit along the axis, that of case II
needs the magnetic field to, and for $m > 1$ these fall at different sizes. At large $x$ both tend to 2 with a
decaying ripple, and the polarization dependence fades.

::: classic bohren-huffman-1983

## The thin wire

For $x \ll 1$ the two cases behave very differently, and the difference is the whole story of metal nanowires. In
case I the field along the axis induces a current along the wire with no charges at any surface; the response is
proportional to $(m^2 - 1)$ and the scattering efficiency grows like $x^3$, with no resonance. In case II the field
across the wire polarises it like a two-dimensional dipole, and the leading coefficient is

$$
a_1^{\mathrm{II}} \approx -\frac{i\pi x^2}{4}\,\frac{m^2 - 1}{m^2 + 1} = -\frac{i\pi x^2}{4}\,\frac{\varepsilon - \varepsilon_h}{\varepsilon + \varepsilon_h}.
$$

The denominator is the two-dimensional analogue of the sphere's $\varepsilon + 2\varepsilon_h$: a metal wire in
vacuum resonates where $\varepsilon = -1$, which for a Drude metal is $\omega = \omega_p/\sqrt{2}$ rather than the
sphere's $\omega_p/\sqrt{3}$. Embedding the wire in a medium of permittivity $\varepsilon_h$ moves the resonance to
$\varepsilon = -\varepsilon_h$. The [wires and fibres](learn/cylinders/wires-and-fibres.html) section follows this
resonance down to a wire one nanometre thick, where the local description reaches its limit.

## Coated cylinders and oblique incidence

A cylinder with shells is solved by the same $2\times 2$ recursion as a multilayered sphere: one transfer matrix per
interface and per order $m$, multiplied inward from the host. PyStratify's cylinder solver does this for any number of
shells, with the amplitudes carried in logarithmic form so that a thick absorbing shell or a high order never
overflows. At **oblique incidence** $k_z = k\cos\zeta$ is no longer zero: $q$ shrinks, every Bessel argument changes,
and, except for $m = 0$, the two polarizations **couple** at each interface, so the transfer matrix becomes $4\times 4$
per order and a case-I wave scatters partly into case-II light. The calculator's incidence angle for cylinders is this
$\zeta$ (90° is normal incidence); the hybrid modes it then finds are the ones that guide light along an optical
fibre, which is the subject of the [wires and fibres](learn/cylinders/wires-and-fibres.html) section.

## How much can one channel scatter? Superscattering

Each order $m$ is a separate channel, and for a lossless cylinder its coefficient can at most reach the value that
makes $|b_m|^2$ (or $|a_m|^2$) equal to 1: the contribution of a single channel to the scattering width is bounded by
$2\lambda/\pi$ (counting $\pm m$ together). A subwavelength object that resonates in one channel can therefore never
scatter more than this, no matter how strong the resonance; it is the two-dimensional analogue of the
single-channel limit of a sphere. Ruan and Fan noticed that nothing stops *several* channels from resonating at the
same wavelength if the structure has enough free parameters, and designed a three-layer plasmonic rod whose $m = 1,
2, 3, 4$ resonances coincide, so that the scattering width exceeds the single-channel bound several times over:
**superscattering**. The design is sensitive by construction, because four resonances have to be tuned onto each
other.

::: classic ruan-fan-2010

records.title: Wires and fibres: emitters beside a cylinder and beams through it
records.summary: A point dipole next to a nanowire or an optical fibre: the continuous spectrum of axial wavenumbers, the guided modes as poles, and how the radiated, guided and absorbed powers are separated. The thin metal wire's plasmon at the local limit. And a fibre under an infrared microscope's Cassegrain: why a fibre that absorbs nothing shows a spectrum.

references.cite: V. V. Klimov and M. Ducloy, Phys. Rev. A 69, 013812 (2004)
A. W. Snyder and J. D. Love, Optical Waveguide Theory (Chapman and Hall, 1983), ch. 12–13
R. Ruppin, Opt. Commun. 190, 205 (2001)
B. J. Davis, P. S. Carney and R. Bhargava, Anal. Chem. 82, 3474 (2010)
B. J. Davis, P. S. Carney and R. Bhargava, Anal. Chem. 83, 525 (2011)
C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles (Wiley, 1983), ch. 8

records.body:
The plane-wave problem of the [previous section](learn/cylinders/infinite-cylinder.html) has a single axial
wavenumber, fixed by the angle of incidence. Two other sources the calculator offers break that simplicity in
instructive ways. A **point dipole** radiates in every direction at once, so its field contains every axial
wavenumber $k_z$ and every order $m$; the cylinder's response must be integrated over $k_z$, and the poles of that
integrand are the guided modes of the wire or fibre. A **focused beam** is a bundle of plane waves filling a cone, and
a cylinder under an infrared microscope answers each of them differently; the spectrum the instrument records is the
cone average.

## A dipole beside a cylinder

Expand the dipole's field in cylindrical waves $e^{im\varphi} e^{ik_z z} H^{(1)}_m(q\rho)$: unlike the plane wave,
which has one $k_z$, the dipole needs all of them, with $q = \sqrt{k^2 - k_z^2}$ passing from real (waves that
propagate away from the axis) to imaginary (waves bound to it) as $|k_z|$ grows past $k$. For each $(m, k_z)$ the
cylinder's transfer matrices give the reflected cylindrical wave at the dipole's position, with the two polarizations
coupled whenever $k_z \ne 0$. The power the dipole radiates, relative to free space, is an integral over $k_z$ and a
sum over $m$ of the work the reflected field does on the dipole, the direct analogue of the Chance–Prock–Silbey
integral for a [dipole near a plane](learn/films/dipole-near-an-interface.html) (Klimov and Ducloy give the complete
formulas for an atom beside a nanofibre).

The integrand has three kinds of contribution, and PyStratify separates them because they are what an experiment
sees separately:

- $|k_z| < k_h$ in the host: cylindrical waves that **radiate** away to the far field;
- **poles** of the reflected amplitude at real $k_z = n_\mathrm{eff} k_0 > k_h$: the guided modes of the fibre
  (HE$_{11}$ first, which has no cutoff, then TE$_{01}$, TM$_{01}$, HE$_{21}$, … as the fibre grows), each taking a
  share of the dipole's power that then travels along the fibre without radiating. In a lossless fibre these poles sit
  on the real axis and the residues are taken analytically, so the guided fraction does not depend on a quadrature
  grid; PyStratify checks the modes it finds against the fibre's closed-form dispersion relations (Snyder and Love);
- the rest of the evanescent range, which against an absorbing wire deposits power in the metal (the quenching
  channel) and against a lossless one contributes nothing to the total but shapes the near field.

A dipole oriented radially, azimuthally or axially couples to different orders $m$ and different modes, so the three
orientations have different rates, and an isotropic ensemble averages them. Close to a metal wire the quenching rises
as $d^{-3}$, as it does near a plane, but the enhancement at the wire's plasmon is sharper, because a thin wire is a
nearly one-dimensional resonator.

## The thin metal wire, and where the local model stops

The case-II resonance of a thin wire sits where $\varepsilon(\omega) = -\varepsilon_h$, that is at $\omega_p/\sqrt{2}$
for a Drude metal in vacuum and $\omega_p/\sqrt{3}$ in a host of $\varepsilon_h = 2$. Ruppin computed the extinction of
a sodium wire one nanometre in radius in two ways: with the local Drude permittivity, which gives exactly this
resonance, and with a hydrodynamic (nonlocal) electron gas, in which the pressure of the electron fluid pushes the
resonance to higher frequency and lets longitudinal bulk plasmons appear above $\omega_p$. The calculator reproduces
the local curve; the nonlocal correction is a different constitutive relation, and it matters only when a dimension
shrinks to a few nanometres or an emitter approaches a surface that closely. For gold and silver particles above
about 10 nm the local model is quantitatively right, and the local curve is the one to compare an experiment with
first.

::: classic ruppin-2001

## A fibre under a Cassegrain

An infrared microscope illuminates its sample through a Cassegrain objective: a cone of plane waves between an inner
obscuration and the outer numerical aperture, each arriving at a different angle $\zeta$ to a fibre lying in the
focal plane. For every angle the oblique-incidence solution of the [previous section](learn/cylinders/infinite-cylinder.html)
gives the field transmitted towards the detector; the instrument's reading is the incoherent average over the cone of
the power collected within its own aperture, and dividing by the empty-field reading gives an apparent absorbance.
Davis, Carney and Bhargava showed that this apparent absorbance of a fibre that **absorbs nothing** is far from zero:
light is refracted and scattered out of the collection cone in a way that depends on wavelength through the size
parameter, so a textile fibre or a hair shows a broad, oscillating baseline with dips where the fibre acts as a lens.
Real absorption bands ride on this baseline, and a quantitative spectrum needs the baseline computed and removed, not
fitted by a polynomial. This is the physics the calculator's focused (Cassegrain) source implements for films,
cylinders and spheres; the sphere version is the Mie-type scattering that distorts the infrared spectra of cells, met
in the [Mie theory](learn/spheres/mie-scattering.html) section.

::: classic davis-2011

Two parameters of the instrument matter and are often left out of a paper's caption: the numerical aperture, which
sets the widest angle in the cone, and the central obscuration of the Cassegrain, which removes the near-normal rays.
Both change the baseline's shape; Davis's Fig. 5 is reproduced with the aperture of the same paper's Fig. 2. The
calculator exposes both, together with the fibre's radius, so the three can be varied against a measured spectrum.

records.title: Mie theory: light scattered by a sphere
records.summary: How a plane wave scatters off a homogeneous sphere: the plane wave as a sum of multipoles, the coefficients a_ℓ and b_ℓ from two boundary conditions per order, the efficiencies and the amplitude functions of the far field, the Rayleigh and geometric limits and the extinction paradox, van de Hulst's anomalous diffraction, where the series stops, and the numerics of the Riccati–Bessel functions that every Mie code lives or dies by.

references.cite: C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles (Wiley, 1983), ch. 4
H. C. van de Hulst, Light Scattering by Small Particles (Wiley, 1957; Dover, 1981), ch. 9 and 11
M. Kerker, The Scattering of Light and Other Electromagnetic Radiation (Academic Press, 1969), ch. 3
W. J. Wiscombe, Appl. Opt. 19, 1505 (1980)
W. J. Lentz, Appl. Opt. 15, 668 (1976)
A. Moroz, Ann. Phys. 315, 352 (2005)
A. I. Kuznetsov et al., Sci. Rep. 2, 492 (2012)

records.body:
A sphere of radius $a$ and refractive index $n_s$ sits in a host of index $n_h$, lit by a plane wave of vacuum
wavelength $\lambda$. Two numbers decide everything that follows: the **size parameter** and the **relative index**,

$$
x = \frac{2\pi n_h a}{\lambda}, \qquad m = \frac{n_s}{n_h}.
$$

Gustav Mie solved this problem exactly in 1908, to explain why colloidal gold is red, violet or blue depending on the
size of its particles (Lorenz had the solution in 1890 and Debye in 1909, which is why the theory carries three
names in the older literature). The same solution describes a raindrop, a silicon nanoparticle and a biological cell
under an infrared microscope, and it is the single-interface case of the
[multilayered sphere](learn/spheres/recursive-transfer-matrix.html) that PyStratify solves in general.

::: classic mie-1908

## The plane wave as a sum of multipoles

In spherical coordinates the vector wave equation separates (the
[Foundations](learn/common/maxwell-and-boundary-conditions.html) table). The fields inside and outside the sphere
become sums of vector spherical harmonics, each labelled by an angular order $\ell = 1, 2, \dots$ (dipole,
quadrupole, …) and by its character: **electric** (transverse magnetic, TM) or **magnetic** (transverse electric,
TE). The first step, and the one that makes the whole method work, is to write the incident plane wave in the same
language. A plane wave polarized along $x$ and travelling along $z$ is (Bohren and Huffman Eq. 4.37)

$$
\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{inc} = E_0\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty} i^\ell\,\frac{2\ell+1}{\ell(\ell+1)}\left(\mathbf{M}^{(1)}_{o1\ell} - i\,\mathbf{N}^{(1)}_{e1\ell}\right),
$$

a sum over orders of the regular ($j_\ell$-based) magnetic and electric multipoles with $m = 1$ only, with the
coefficients $E_\ell = i^\ell E_0 (2\ell+1)/[\ell(\ell+1)]$. Only $|m| = 1$ appears because a plane wave has one
axis; a [dipole source](learn/spheres/dipole-near-a-sphere.html) off the centre excites every $m$. The radial
dependence of every term obeys the spherical Bessel equation, a second-order linear equation, so in each region it
is a combination of two independent solutions. We use the Riccati–Bessel functions

$$
\psi_\ell(\rho) = \rho\, j_\ell(\rho), \qquad \xi_\ell(\rho) = \rho\, h^{(1)}_\ell(\rho),
$$

regular at the centre and outgoing at infinity respectively: inside the sphere only $\psi_\ell$ is allowed, outside the
scattered field is pure $\xi_\ell$, and the incident field is $\psi_\ell$.

## Two boundary conditions per order

At $r = a$ the tangential components of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ are continuous. Because the harmonics are
orthogonal on the sphere, the conditions hold order by order and character by character: for each $\ell$ and each
of TM and TE this gives two linear equations in two unknowns (the internal amplitude and the scattered one), the
same $2\times 2$ structure as a single interface of a thin film. Solving them gives the scattering coefficients of a
non-magnetic sphere (time dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$):

$$
a_\ell = \frac{m\,\psi_\ell(mx)\,\psi_\ell'(x) - \psi_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(mx)}{m\,\psi_\ell(mx)\,\xi_\ell'(x) - \xi_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(mx)},
\qquad
b_\ell = \frac{\psi_\ell(mx)\,\psi_\ell'(x) - m\,\psi_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(mx)}{\psi_\ell(mx)\,\xi_\ell'(x) - m\,\xi_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(mx)}.
$$

$a_\ell$ is the electric multipole of order $\ell$, $b_\ell$ the magnetic one, and the two differ only in where the
relative index $m$ sits, exactly as $r_s$ and $r_p$ of a film differ in where $n$ sits. For a magnetic sphere ($\mu
\ne 1$) $m$ in the numerators and denominators is replaced by $m/\mu$ or $m\mu$ in the appropriate places (Kerker's
book), which is how a sphere with $\varepsilon = \mu$ comes to have $a_\ell = b_\ell$, the origin of the Kerker
conditions of the [next section](learn/spheres/multipoles.html). The resonances of the sphere live in the
denominators: where one nearly vanishes, its coefficient peaks and the sphere radiates strongly in that multipole.
Add shells and each interface contributes one more $2\times 2$ matrix; that is the transfer-matrix solution of the
multilayered sphere, and what PyStratify computes for any number of layers.

## Efficiencies and the far field

Dividing the cross sections by the geometric area $\pi a^2$ gives the efficiencies:

$$
Q_\mathrm{sca} = \frac{2}{x^2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(2\ell+1)\left(|a_\ell|^2 + |b_\ell|^2\right),
\qquad
Q_\mathrm{ext} = \frac{2}{x^2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(2\ell+1)\,\mathrm{Re}\,(a_\ell + b_\ell),
$$

and $Q_\mathrm{abs} = Q_\mathrm{ext} - Q_\mathrm{sca}$. Each term of the sums is the share of one multipole, which is
how the calculator splits a spectrum into its electric and magnetic orders. The extinction formula is the **optical
theorem** in disguise: $Q_\mathrm{ext}$ is the forward-scattering amplitude's imaginary part, so the light removed from
the beam is measured by what is scattered exactly forward, whether the sphere absorbs or not. The angular
distribution comes from the two **amplitude functions**

$$
S_1(\theta) = \sum_\ell \frac{2\ell+1}{\ell(\ell+1)}\left(a_\ell\,\pi_\ell + b_\ell\,\tau_\ell\right),
\qquad
S_2(\theta) = \sum_\ell \frac{2\ell+1}{\ell(\ell+1)}\left(a_\ell\,\tau_\ell + b_\ell\,\pi_\ell\right),
$$

with $\pi_\ell = P_\ell^1/\sin\theta$ and $\tau_\ell = \mathrm{d}P_\ell^1/\mathrm{d}\theta$ the angular functions; the
scattered intensity for light polarized perpendicular and parallel to the scattering plane is $|S_1|^2$ and
$|S_2|^2$ over $(ka)^2$, and the polarization, the asymmetry parameter $\langle\cos\theta\rangle$ and the Mueller
matrix all follow from them. Checks of the engine's $S_1$, $S_2$ against Bohren and Huffman's own BHMIE and against
two other Mie codes are on the [Verification](verification.html) page.

## A silicon sphere

Silicon has an index near 4 across the visible. Inside so dense a particle the wavelength shrinks to $\lambda/n_s$, and
when it becomes comparable to the diameter the field inside circulates: a loop of displacement current, the
**magnetic dipole** $b_1$. It is the lowest resonance of a high-index sphere, longer in wavelength than the electric
dipole $a_1$ that follows it, and it gives such particles their colours (Kuznetsov et al., 2012).

::: example si-sphere-mie

Move the radius from 50 to 135 nm and the magnetic dipole walks across the visible spectrum; the electric dipole and
then the magnetic quadrupole follow it at shorter wavelengths.

## Where the series stops

The sums converge once $\ell$ exceeds the size parameter by a few terms: a partial wave of order $\ell$ has its
angular momentum at an impact parameter $\ell/k$, and orders with $\ell/k \gg a$ miss the sphere. Wiscombe's rule

$$
\ell_\mathrm{max} = x + 4x^{1/3} + 2
$$

is accurate for far-field quantities to about $10^{-8}$; the $x^{1/3}$ term is the width of the edge region where
grazing partial waves are diffracted. For a high-index core the internal size parameter $|m|x$ matters as well, so
PyStratify, and the calculator through it, take the larger of the two; a field evaluated at the surface, or a
[dipole close to it](learn/spheres/dipole-near-a-sphere.html), needs more still, and the engine extends the order
until the quantity converges.

## The numerics every Mie code lives by

Mie's formulas are exact and innocent-looking, and most of the published Mie codes that give wrong answers fail in
the Riccati–Bessel functions, not in the physics. Three facts matter. $\psi_\ell(z)$ computed by *upward* recurrence
in $\ell$ is unstable for $\ell > |z|$ (the errors grow like the ratio of the two solutions, which is huge there), so
the standard trick since Deirmendjian is to compute the **logarithmic derivative** $D_\ell(mx) = \psi_\ell'(mx)/\psi_\ell(mx)$
by *downward* recurrence from a starting order well above $\ell_\mathrm{max}$, or by Lentz's continued fraction
(1976), and to write $a_\ell$ and $b_\ell$ in terms of $D_\ell$ alone; this is BHMIE's algorithm. For complex $mx$ the
function $\psi_\ell(mx)$ itself grows like $e^{|\mathrm{Im}\,mx|}$, and the coefficients are ratios of numbers that
overflow long before the sums converge, which is where a **logarithmic** representation of the amplitudes, carried
through the transfer-matrix recursion (Moroz 2005), keeps a metal sphere or a thin absorbing shell safe at any order.
And for $\ell \gg x$ the coefficients fall like $(x/\ell)^{4\ell}$, so a sum that is stopped early is wrong by the
first dropped term, not by a rounding error; a coefficient of $10^{-300}$ must be representable, or set to exactly
zero, never to garbage. The [Verification](verification.html) page compares the engine's coefficients with the same
formulas evaluated in 60-digit arithmetic over forty orders of a thin nanoshell, and with BHMIE to $x = 20\,000$; one of
those comparisons found BHMIE's own double-precision recurrence drifting at large $x$ for a weakly absorbing sphere.

## Two limits worth knowing

For a sphere much smaller than the wavelength ($x \ll 1$) only $a_1$ survives, with
$a_1 \approx -\tfrac{2i}{3}x^3\,\frac{m^2-1}{m^2+2}$, and

$$
Q_\mathrm{sca} \approx \frac{8}{3}\,x^4 \left|\frac{m^2 - 1}{m^2 + 2}\right|^2,
\qquad
Q_\mathrm{abs} \approx 4x\,\mathrm{Im}\,\frac{m^2 - 1}{m^2 + 2} ,
$$

Rayleigh's $\lambda^{-4}$ law for scattering, and an absorption that goes as the *volume*, so that small absorbing
particles absorb far more than they scatter. For a metal the denominator vanishes near $\varepsilon_s = -2\varepsilon_h$:
that is the localized surface plasmon of a small gold or silver particle, at 520 nm for gold in water, the colour of
the ruby glass that started Mie on the problem. For a sphere much larger than the wavelength, $Q_\mathrm{ext} \to 2$:
the sphere removes twice the light that falls on its cross section, half by absorption or reflection and half by
diffraction around its edge, the **extinction paradox**, resolved by noting that the diffracted half is scattered into
so narrow a forward cone that any real detector collects it and measures $Q \approx 1$. Between the two limits a weakly
refracting sphere ($m \to 1$, $x \gg 1$) follows van de Hulst's anomalous-diffraction approximation,
$Q_\mathrm{ext} \approx 2 - \frac{4}{\rho}\sin\rho + \frac{4}{\rho^2}(1 - \cos\rho)$ with the phase lag $\rho = 2x(m-1)$:
a slow oscillation in wavelength, with its first maximum near $\rho = 4$, that a cell or a nucleus of a few
micrometres imprints on its infrared spectrum, and which is routinely mistaken for a baseline.

::: classic mohlenhoff-2005

records.title: Multipoles, directional scattering and the Kerker conditions
records.summary: Reading a spectrum by its electric and magnetic multipoles: each order's share of the scattering and the single-channel bound, the small-sphere expansions of a_1 and b_1, how a magnetic dipole arises in a dielectric and where it sits, the forward and backward amplitudes, the first and second Kerker conditions and their generalisation to quadrupoles, Huygens metasurfaces, and the anapole as a zero of a_1.

references.cite: C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles (Wiley, 1983), ch. 4
M. Kerker, D.-S. Wang and C. L. Giles, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 73, 765 (1983)
A. B. Evlyukhin, C. Reinhardt, A. Seidel, B. S. Luk'yanchuk and B. N. Chichkov, Phys. Rev. B 82, 045404 (2010)
A. I. Kuznetsov et al., Sci. Rep. 2, 492 (2012)
J. M. Geffrin et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1171 (2012)
Y. H. Fu et al., Nat. Commun. 4, 1527 (2013)
I. Staude et al., ACS Nano 7, 7824 (2013)
A. E. Miroshnichenko et al., Nat. Commun. 6, 8069 (2015)

records.body:
The Mie series is a sum over multipoles, and every term has a physical identity: $a_\ell$ is the electric multipole
of order $\ell$ (dipole, quadrupole, …), $b_\ell$ the magnetic one. Taking a spectrum apart term by term turns a
curve with many bumps into a short list of resonances, each with its own field pattern and its own radiation
diagram, and the interference of those diagrams is what makes a particle scatter forward, backward, or not at all.
This is the vocabulary of all-dielectric nanophotonics, and it is a few lines of algebra on the
[Mie coefficients](learn/spheres/mie-scattering.html).

## Each order's share

Because the vector spherical harmonics are orthogonal over the sphere, the scattered power is a plain sum over orders
and types, with no cross terms:

$$
Q_\mathrm{sca} = \sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty} \left(Q^{E}_{\ell} + Q^{M}_{\ell}\right),
\qquad
Q^{E}_{\ell} = \frac{2}{x^2}(2\ell+1)\,|a_\ell|^2,
\qquad
Q^{M}_{\ell} = \frac{2}{x^2}(2\ell+1)\,|b_\ell|^2 .
$$

Each term is bounded: a single channel cannot scatter more than $\frac{2}{x^2}(2\ell+1)$, the limit reached when
$|a_\ell| = 1$, which for a lossless sphere is where the coefficient's phase passes through $\pi/2$ at a resonance.
In cross-section terms the bound is $(2\ell+1)\lambda^2/(2\pi)$ per channel: a dipole, however resonant, cannot
scatter more than $3\lambda^2/2\pi$, which is why a 10 nm silver particle at its plasmon has a cross section a
hundred times its geometric one and no more. Extinction splits the same way, through $\mathrm{Re}\,a_\ell$ and
$\mathrm{Re}\,b_\ell$; the calculator's multipole panel draws these shares, one colour per order, electric dashed
and magnetic dot-dashed.

## The small sphere: what a_1 and b_1 are made of

Expanding the coefficients in the size parameter shows what each resonance is physically. To leading orders,

$$
a_1 \approx -\frac{2i}{3}\,x^3\,\frac{m^2-1}{m^2+2}\left[1 + \frac{3}{5}\,\frac{m^2 - 2}{m^2 + 2}\,x^2 + \dots\right],
\qquad
b_1 \approx -\frac{i}{45}\,x^5\,(m^2-1) ,
\qquad
a_2 \approx -\frac{i}{15}\,x^5\,\frac{m^2-1}{2m^2+3} .
$$

The electric dipole is the quasi-static polarizability of a sphere, with the Clausius–Mossotti denominator and its
plasmon pole at $m^2 = -2$; the magnetic dipole has no pole in the quasi-static limit and starts two powers of $x$
later, at the same order as the electric quadrupole. For a metal the first term is everything and the particle is an
electric dipole; for a dielectric the $x^2$ correction inside the bracket and the $x^5$ terms grow quickly with $m$,
and at $mx \sim \pi$ the expansion fails altogether, because the magnetic dipole resonates.

## A magnetic dipole without magnetism

Silicon has $\mu = 1$, yet a silicon sphere has a strong magnetic-dipole resonance. When the wavelength inside the
particle, $\lambda/n$, is close to its diameter, the electric field inside circulates around an axis perpendicular to
the incident field. That loop of displacement current is a magnetic dipole, and in a high-index sphere it is the
first resonance on the long-wavelength side: the condition is $\lambda_\mathrm{MD} \approx n_s\, d$, the first zero of
the magnetic denominator at $mx \approx \pi$ for large $m$ (Evlyukhin et al. 2010), so a 150 nm silicon sphere resonates
near 600 nm. The electric dipole sits at shorter wavelength ($mx \approx 4.5$), the magnetic quadrupole between them.
Kuznetsov et al. (2012) saw the magnetic dipole move across the visible as the particles grew, giving them their
colours, and Geffrin et al. (2012) measured the same resonances in the microwave range with centimetre-sized
ceramic spheres, where the far-field pattern can be mapped directly.

::: example si-sphere-multipoles

Move the radius and watch the order: magnetic dipole first, then electric dipole and magnetic quadrupole close
together, then the electric quadrupole. The electric dipole is broad because it also radiates from the particle's
polarization outside the resonance; the magnetic modes, confined inside the sphere, are narrower.

::: classic kuznetsov-2012

## Forward and backward

The far field in the forward and backward directions follows from the same coefficients, because at $\theta = 0$ and
$\pi$ the angular functions $\pi_\ell$ and $\tau_\ell$ both equal $\pm\ell(\ell+1)/2$:

$$
Q_\mathrm{f} = \frac{1}{x^2}\left|\sum_\ell (2\ell+1)(a_\ell + b_\ell)\right|^2,
\qquad
Q_\mathrm{b} = \frac{1}{x^2}\left|\sum_\ell (2\ell+1)(-1)^\ell (a_\ell - b_\ell)\right|^2 .
$$

Electric and magnetic multipoles of the same order add in the forward direction and subtract backwards: an electric
dipole and a magnetic dipole, crossed and in phase, radiate like a Huygens source, forward only. If only the dipoles
matter and $a_1 = b_1$, the backscattering vanishes: the **first Kerker condition**, found by Kerker, Wang and Giles
(1983) for spheres with $\varepsilon = \mu$, where every $a_\ell$ equals its $b_\ell$ and the sphere does not
backscatter at any size. A dielectric sphere has no $\mu$, but it reaches $a_1 = b_1$ at one wavelength where its
electric- and magnetic-dipole curves cross on the long-wavelength side of the magnetic resonance, and there it
scatters forward almost only (Fu et al. 2013; Geffrin et al. 2012 saw the same in the microwave). The **second Kerker
condition**, $a_1 = -b_1$, minimises forward scattering, but cannot null it: the optical theorem ties forward
scattering to the extinction, which is never zero. With quadrupoles the conditions generalise to the full sums,
$\sum_\ell (2\ell+1)(-1)^\ell(a_\ell - b_\ell) = 0$ for zero backscattering, which can be met at more than one
wavelength and with a sharper directivity; the forward-to-backward ratio of the classic card is the number to watch.

::: classic fu-2013

## From one sphere to a Huygens surface

A sphere at its first Kerker condition transmits all the light it intercepts, with a phase delay set by the two
resonances. An array of such spheres, one per sub-wavelength cell, is a **Huygens metasurface** (Staude et al. 2013): a
flat sheet with near-unit transmittance whose phase can be chosen from $0$ to $2\pi$ by the particle size, the
building block of flat lenses and holograms. Its design reduces to placing the electric and magnetic dipole
resonances of the single particle, which is the calculation above, with the lattice adding a correction that the
single-sphere calculation leaves out.

## Beyond the dipoles

When an electric dipole and a toroidal dipole of the same strength radiate in antiphase, their far fields cancel and
the electric-dipole scattering nearly vanishes while the field inside stays strong: the anapole (Miroshnichenko et al.,
2015). In the Mie picture it is simply a zero of $a_1$, visible in the decomposition as a dip of the electric dipole
between resonances: the full coefficient contains both the Cartesian electric dipole and the toroidal moment, and the
multipole expansion in vector spherical harmonics, being complete, needs no separate toroidal term. The distinction
matters when one wants to know what is going on *inside* the particle (a toroidal field pattern) rather than what it
radiates, and the near-field panel of the calculator shows exactly that circulating pattern at the anapole
wavelength.

records.title: The multilayered sphere: a recursive transfer matrix
records.summary: Mie's solution extended to any number of concentric shells: the fields of each shell as regular and outgoing multipoles, the 2×2 transfer matrix of one interface written in Riccati–Bessel functions, raising and lowering through the shells, the two conditions that close the system, and the numerical discipline (logarithmic amplitudes, ratios of Bessel functions) that makes thousands of orders and nanometre shells safe. Plasmon hybridization in a nanoshell as the first application.

references.cite: A. L. Aden and M. Kerker, J. Appl. Phys. 22, 1242 (1951)
A. Moroz, Ann. Phys. 315, 352 (2005)
I. L. Rasskazov, P. S. Carney and A. Moroz, OSA Continuum 3, 2290 (2020)
W. Yang, Appl. Opt. 42, 1710 (2003)
O. Peña and U. Pal, Comput. Phys. Commun. 180, 2348 (2009)
E. Prodan, C. Radloff, N. J. Halas and P. Nordlander, Science 302, 419 (2003)
C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles (Wiley, 1983), §8.1

records.body:
Aden and Kerker solved the coated sphere in 1951 by writing out the boundary conditions at both interfaces and
inverting the resulting $4\times 4$ system. For a nanomatryoshka with four shells that route gives an $8\times 8$
system, for a graded profile sampled in a hundred steps it is hopeless, and in every case the direct inversion is
numerically fragile. The transfer-matrix formulation of the [Foundations](learn/common/why-transfer-matrices.html)
chapter does better: one $2\times 2$ matrix per interface and per channel, multiplied inward or outward, with the
same code for a plane wave and for a dipole inside or outside any shell. This section writes that recursion down in the
form PyStratify implements, following Moroz (2005) and the STRATIFY paper.

## The fields in each shell

Number the regions from the core outward, $n = 1, \dots, N + 1$, the host being $N + 1$; region $n$ has index $n_n$,
wavenumber $k_n = n_n k_0$ and permeability $\mu_n$, and the interface between $n$ and $n + 1$ sits at $r_n$. In each
region the electric field is a sum over the composite angular index $L = (\ell, m)$ and the two polarizations
$p = M$ (magnetic, TE) and $p = E$ (electric, TM) of a regular and an outgoing multipole,

$$
\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{p, L}\left[A_{pL}(n)\,\mathbf{J}_{pL}(k_n, \mathbf{r}) + B_{pL}(n)\,\mathbf{H}_{pL}(k_n, \mathbf{r})\right],
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ are the vector multipole fields built on $j_\ell$ and $h^{(1)}_\ell$ with the
normalised vector spherical harmonics $\mathbf{Y}^{(m)}_L$, $\mathbf{Y}^{(e)}_L$, $\mathbf{Y}^{(o)}_L$ (Jackson's; Bohren
and Huffman's $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{N}$ give the same results). The magnetic field follows from
$\mathbf{H} = -i\sqrt{\varepsilon_n/\mu_n}\,\nabla\times\mathbf{E}/k_n$, which swaps $\mathbf{J}_{ML}$ and
$\mathbf{J}_{EL}$: the magnetic multipole's $\mathbf{H}$ looks like an electric multipole's $\mathbf{E}$, and vice
versa. The amplitudes $A_{pL}(n)$, $B_{pL}(n)$ are the unknowns, two per region, per $\ell$, per polarization. Because
the harmonics are orthogonal and the problem has spherical symmetry, nothing couples different $L$ or different $p$:
every channel $(p, \ell)$ is a scalar problem of the Foundations type, and $m$ never appears in the matrices.

## The transfer matrix of one interface

Continuity of the tangential $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ at $r_n$ links the amplitudes on both sides. With the
Riccati–Bessel functions $\psi_\ell(z) = z\, j_\ell(z)$, $\zeta_\ell(z) = z\, h^{(1)}_\ell(z)$, the internal size
parameter $x_n = k_n r_n$, the external one $\tilde{x}_n = k_{n+1} r_n$, and the relative index and permeability
$\tilde{\eta}_n = n_n / n_{n+1}$, $\tilde{\mu}_n = \mu_n/\mu_{n+1}$, the **lowering** matrix that carries the outer
amplitudes to the inner ones for a magnetic multipole is

$$
\begin{pmatrix} A_{ML}(n) \\ B_{ML}(n) \end{pmatrix} = T^-_{M\ell}(n) \begin{pmatrix} A_{ML}(n+1) \\ B_{ML}(n+1) \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T^-_{M\ell}(n) = -i
\begin{pmatrix}
\tilde{\eta}\,\zeta_\ell'(x)\,\psi_\ell(\tilde{x}) - \tilde{\mu}\,\zeta_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(\tilde{x})
& \tilde{\eta}\,\zeta_\ell'(x)\,\zeta_\ell(\tilde{x}) - \tilde{\mu}\,\zeta_\ell(x)\,\zeta_\ell'(\tilde{x}) \\
-\tilde{\eta}\,\psi_\ell'(x)\,\psi_\ell(\tilde{x}) + \tilde{\mu}\,\psi_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(\tilde{x})
& -\tilde{\eta}\,\psi_\ell'(x)\,\zeta_\ell(\tilde{x}) + \tilde{\mu}\,\psi_\ell(x)\,\zeta_\ell'(\tilde{x})
\end{pmatrix},
$$

with $x = x_n$, $\tilde{x} = \tilde{x}_n$ and the subscript $n$ dropped on $\tilde{\eta}$, $\tilde{\mu}$. The electric
matrix $T^-_{E\ell}$ is the same expression with $\tilde{\eta}$ and $\tilde{\mu}$ interchanged, and the **raising**
matrices $T^+ = (T^-)^{-1}$ have the same shape with the roles of $x$ and $\tilde{x}$ exchanged and $\tilde{\eta}$,
$\tilde{\mu}$ in the denominators. The prefactor $-i$ is the inverse Wronskian $\psi_\ell\zeta_\ell' -
\psi_\ell'\zeta_\ell = i$, which is what makes the matrix exactly invertible; $\det T^\pm = \tilde{\eta}\tilde{\mu}$
up to the normalisation of the fields, never zero.

## Raising, lowering, and the two closing conditions

Multiplying the matrices of successive interfaces moves the pair of amplitudes through the whole onion:

$$
\begin{pmatrix} A_{pL}(n) \\ B_{pL}(n) \end{pmatrix} = \mathcal{T}_{p\ell}(n)\begin{pmatrix} A_{pL}(1) \\ B_{pL}(1) \end{pmatrix},
\quad \mathcal{T}_{p\ell}(n) = \prod_{j = n-1}^{1} T^+_{p\ell}(j);
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix} A_{pL}(n) \\ B_{pL}(n) \end{pmatrix} = \mathcal{M}_{p\ell}(n)\begin{pmatrix} A_{pL}(N+1) \\ B_{pL}(N+1) \end{pmatrix},
\quad \mathcal{M}_{p\ell}(n) = \prod_{j = n}^{N} T^-_{p\ell}(j),
$$

with $\mathcal{M}_{p\ell}(1) = \mathcal{T}_{p\ell}(N+1)^{-1}$. For $N$ interfaces these are $2N$ equations for
$2(N+1)$ amplitudes per channel; two more conditions close the system:

- **regularity at the centre**: no outgoing (singular) wave emerges from the origin unless a source sits there, so
  $B_{pL}(1) = 0$;
- **the source**: for a plane wave, the regular amplitude in the host is the known expansion of the incident wave,
  $A_{pL}(N+1) = A^{\mathrm{inc}}_{pL}$, and the outgoing amplitude $B_{pL}(N+1)$ is the scattered wave.

Writing $\mathcal{T}_{p\ell}(N+1) = \begin{pmatrix} \mathcal{T}_{11} & \mathcal{T}_{12} \\ \mathcal{T}_{21} &
\mathcal{T}_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ and applying both conditions gives the scattered amplitude in one line,

$$
B_{pL}(N+1) = \frac{\mathcal{T}_{21}}{\mathcal{T}_{11}}\, A_{pL}(N+1) ,
$$

so the whole multilayered sphere has been reduced to a homogeneous one with **composite Mie coefficients**
$a_\ell, b_\ell = \mathcal{T}_{21}/\mathcal{T}_{11}$ (up to the sign convention of the outgoing wave). Every far-field
formula of [Mie theory](learn/spheres/mie-scattering.html), the efficiencies, the scattering pattern, the
[multipole decomposition](learn/spheres/multipoles.html), the Kerker conditions, holds unchanged with these
coefficients; the near field in any shell is read off from the amplitudes $\mathcal{T}(n)$ produced on the way. A
**dipole source** in shell $n_d$ changes only the second condition: the outgoing amplitude jumps by the dipole's own
multipole expansion at $r_d$, and "no incoming wave from infinity" replaces the plane wave; the matrices are the same.
That is the subject of the [next section](learn/spheres/dipole-near-a-sphere.html).

## Numerical discipline

The elegance of the recursion hides two traps that have broken many published codes.

**Growth of the Riccati–Bessel functions.** For complex argument $z$, $\zeta_\ell(z)$ grows like $e^{|\mathrm{Im}\,z|}$
and $\psi_\ell(z)$ like $e^{|\mathrm{Im}\,z|}$ too, while for $|z| \ll \ell$ the pair behaves as $z^{\ell+1}$ and
$z^{-\ell}$: inside a metal shell or at high orders, the matrix elements span hundreds of orders of magnitude and the
products lose every digit or overflow. Yang's "improved recursive algorithm" and scattnlay avoid the worst of it with
ratios and logarithmic derivatives of the Bessel functions. PyStratify goes one step further and carries each
amplitude together with its logarithm, so that the growing factors are divided out before any product is formed and a
sphere with a 2 nm silver shell at $\ell = 500$ is as safe as a glass bead at $\ell = 5$. The
[Verification](verification.html) page compares this recursion with the same formulas evaluated in 60-digit
arithmetic, and with scattnlay and treams, down to $10^{-11}$ in the cross sections and $10^{-13}$ in the fields.
