**Truncation and the internal size parameter.** Wiscombe's rule for the number of orders, $\ell_\mathrm{max} = x +
4x^{1/3} + 2$ with $x$ the host size parameter, is designed for the far field of a homogeneous sphere. A high-index
core, where the internal wavelength is short, and a dipole close to a surface both need more orders, so the engine
takes the largest internal $|m| x$ into account and, for emitters, continues until the rates converge. The order
count the calculator reports is this adaptive one.

## The first application: plasmon hybridization

A metal shell on a dielectric core has two surfaces, and each supports a plasmon, that of a cavity in the metal and
that of a sphere of metal. In a thin shell the two couple and split into a low-energy **bonding** and a high-energy
**antibonding** mode, whose separation grows as the shell thins: the nanoshell's resonance can be tuned from the
visible deep into the near infrared with the shell thickness alone, which is the basis of its use in photothermal
therapy. Prodan, Radloff, Halas and Nordlander described this with a hybridization picture borrowed from molecular
orbital theory, and demonstrated it on a **nanomatryoshka**, a nanoshell inside a nanoshell, whose two shell plasmons
hybridize once more when the dielectric spacer between them is thin. In the transfer-matrix language all of this is
in the composite coefficient $a_1$: four interfaces, four matrices, and the zeros of $\mathcal{T}_{11}$ in the complex
frequency plane are the hybridized modes.

::: classic prodan-2003

records.title: A dipole near a sphere: decay rates, quenching and enhancement
records.summary: A molecule or quantum dot beside, or inside, a sphere: how its field is expanded in multipoles, how the sphere's transfer matrices return it, the radiative and non-radiative decay rates that result, the quantum yield, and the competition between enhancement and quenching that fixes the best distance for enhanced fluorescence.

references.cite: R. Ruppin, J. Chem. Phys. 76, 1681 (1982)
H. Chew, J. Chem. Phys. 87, 1355 (1987)
Y. S. Kim, P. T. Leung and T. F. George, Surf. Sci. 195, 1 (1988)
A. Moroz, Ann. Phys. 315, 352 (2005)
R. Carminati, J.-J. Greffet, C. Henkel and J. M. Vigoureux, Opt. Commun. 261, 368 (2006)
P. Anger, P. Bharadwaj and L. Novotny, Phys. Rev. Lett. 96, 113002 (2006)
L. Novotny and B. Hecht, Principles of Nano-Optics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge University Press, 2012), ch. 8

records.body:
A metal nanoparticle next to a fluorescent molecule can make it brighter by an order of magnitude or switch it off
completely, and the difference is a few nanometres of distance. Both effects come out of the same calculation: the
dipole's own field, reflected by the sphere, acts back on the dipole. The sphere's response is the set of
[transfer matrices](learn/spheres/recursive-transfer-matrix.html) already built for the plane wave; only the source
changes, from a wave arriving from infinity to a singular outgoing wave at the dipole's position. Ruppin's 1982 paper
did this for a molecule beside a small silver sphere, Chew's 1987 paper gave the closed expressions used ever since,
and Kim, Leung and George extended them to a dipole inside a coated sphere.

## The dipole's field as outgoing multipoles

An electric dipole $\mathbf{p}$ at $\mathbf{r}_d$ radiates the field of a point source, which, seen from the sphere's
centre, is a sum of outgoing multipoles $\mathbf{H}_{pL}(k, \mathbf{r})$ for $r > r_d$ and of regular ones for
$r < r_d$, with known coefficients (the expansion of the free-space Green dyadic). A dipole therefore enters the
transfer-matrix recursion as a **jump in the amplitudes** at the radius $r_d$: between the inside and the outside of
the shell that contains it, $A_{pL}$ and $B_{pL}$ change by the dipole's own multipole coefficients. The two closing
conditions are regularity at the centre, $B_{pL}(1) = 0$, and no incoming wave from infinity, $A_{pL}(N+1) = 0$. Solving
the $2\times 2$ system per channel gives the field everywhere, and in particular the reflected field at the dipole,
which is what decides its fate.

Unlike a plane wave, which excites only $m = \pm 1$, a dipole off the centre excites every $m$ for each $\ell$, and
a dipole close to the surface excites high $\ell$ strongly, because the near field of a point source is rich in
short-wavelength harmonics. The sums below therefore converge slowly at small distances, and the engine extends the
number of orders until they do.

## Radiative and non-radiative rates

The power the dipole radiates to the far field, relative to the same dipole in the unbounded host, is a sum over
orders of the squared total exterior field amplitudes at the dipole's radius. For a dipole outside a sphere at
distance $r_d$ from the centre, with $z = k_h r_d$ and the Riccati–Bessel functions $\psi_\ell$, $\xi_\ell$, Chew's
results read, for the **radial** (perpendicular) and **tangential** (parallel) orientations,

$$
\frac{\Gamma^\mathrm{rad}_\perp}{\Gamma_0} = \frac{3}{2 z^4}\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty} \ell(\ell+1)(2\ell+1)\,\bigl|\psi_\ell(z) + a_\ell\,\xi_\ell(z)\bigr|^2,
\qquad
\frac{\Gamma^\mathrm{rad}_\parallel}{\Gamma_0} = \frac{3}{4 z^2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty} (2\ell+1)\left[\bigl|\psi_\ell'(z) + a_\ell\,\xi_\ell'(z)\bigr|^2 + \bigl|\psi_\ell(z) + b_\ell\,\xi_\ell(z)\bigr|^2\right],
$$

where $a_\ell$, $b_\ell$ are the sphere's (composite) Mie coefficients in the convention in which the total exterior
field of order $\ell$ is $\psi_\ell + a_\ell\xi_\ell$. A radial dipole drives electric multipoles only; a tangential one
drives both. Far from the sphere ($z \to \infty$) the brackets oscillate about $\psi_\ell$ and the rates tend to
$\Gamma_0$ with a decaying ripple of period half a wavelength, the spherical version of Drexhage's oscillations.

An absorbing sphere also takes power that never reaches the far field: the dipole's near field drives currents in the
metal. The **non-radiative** rate is this absorbed power, obtained either from Poynting's theorem on a surface just
inside the sphere, or as the total rate minus the radiative one, where the total follows from the imaginary part of the
reflected field at the dipole, $\Gamma^\mathrm{tot}/\Gamma_0 = 1 + \tfrac{6\pi}{k^3}\,\mathrm{Im}\,[\hat{\mathbf{p}}\cdot
\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{refl}(\mathbf{r}_d)]/|\mathbf{p}|$ in the normalisation of Novotny and Hecht. PyStratify computes
the three rates separately and reports the total as their sum, which is a check in itself: for a lossless sphere the
non-radiative rate must vanish to machine precision.

## Quenching, enhancement and the best distance

Two opposite trends meet at the surface of a metal sphere. The **radiative** rate is enhanced near the particle's
plasmon resonance, because the sphere acts as an antenna that radiates the dipole's near field efficiently, and the
enhancement reaches further out for a larger sphere. The **non-radiative** rate grows without bound as the dipole
approaches the surface, like $d^{-3}$ in the quasi-static limit for a local metal, because the high-$\ell$ multipoles
that a nearby dipole excites are dark: they store the energy in the metal and dissipate it. The quantum yield of the
coupled system,

$$
q = \frac{\Gamma^\mathrm{rad}}{\Gamma^\mathrm{rad} + \Gamma^\mathrm{nr} + \Gamma_0(1 - q_0)/q_0},
$$

therefore collapses within the first few nanometres (this is quenching), rises to a maximum at a distance of the order
of the particle's radius, and returns to the intrinsic yield $q_0$ far away. The maximum sits further out for a larger
sphere, which Anger, Bharadwaj and Novotny measured by scanning a gold particle over a single molecule: an 80 nm
sphere enhances the fluorescence by a factor of several at about 5 nm, a 20 nm sphere mostly quenches. Fluorescence
is the product of two factors, the excitation rate, proportional to the local plane-wave intensity $|\mathbf{E}|^2$ at
the molecule, and the quantum yield; both are sphere calculations, one with a plane wave and one with a dipole, and
the calculator runs them with the same inputs.

::: classic anger-2006

::: classic ruppin-1982

## Inside a sphere, and in a shell

A dipole **inside** a sphere, or in one of its shells, is handled by the same recursion with the jump placed in that
shell; the radiative rate then involves the amplitudes transmitted to the host, and the formula gains the host's
and the shell's indices as prefactors (Chew; Kim, Leung and George). This is the model of a dye molecule inside a
silica bead, of an emitter in the dielectric spacer of a nanomatryoshka, and, with the sphere of the size of a cell,
of the autofluorescence seen through a microscope. An emitter in a lossless dielectric sphere shows no quenching at
all, only the oscillation of the radiative rate with position and the sharp enhancements at the sphere's
whispering-gallery resonances, which for a large sphere of high index can reach factors of thousands over a narrow
band: the Purcell effect in its original form.

## What the model leaves out

The emitter is a point dipole of fixed frequency and the metal a local, homogeneous medium with a bulk permittivity;
within a nanometre or two of the surface the electron gas's nonlocal response, electron spill-out and the discreteness of
the lattice change the quenching law, and the calculated rate at contact is a limit rather than a prediction. A
dielectric host surrounding the dipole must be lossless for the free-space rate $\Gamma_0$ to be defined. Within those
limits the formulas above are exact, and the [Verification](verification.html) page lists their checks against
independently written Sommerfeld-type integrals, against smuthi and treams, and against the finite-difference and
finite-element methods that know nothing about multipoles.

records.title: Maxwell's equations, boundary conditions and the wave equation
records.summary: The equations every page of this site rests on: Maxwell's equations in a piecewise homogeneous medium, the time convention, the continuity of tangential E and H at an interface, and how separation of variables turns the vector problem for a film, a cylinder or a sphere into one scalar second-order equation per channel.

references.cite: J. D. Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 1999), ch. 7 and §9.7
J. A. Stratton, Electromagnetic Theory (McGraw-Hill, 1941), ch. VI–VII and IX
M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §1.1–1.6
C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles (Wiley, 1983), ch. 2–4 and 8
A. Moroz, Ann. Phys. 315, 352 (2005)
I. L. Rasskazov, P. S. Carney and A. Moroz, OSA Continuum 3, 2290 (2020)

records.body:
Everything the calculator computes, for a thin-film stack, a coated cylinder or a multilayered sphere, lit by a plane
wave, a point dipole or a focused beam, follows from the same four equations and the same two boundary conditions.
This section states them once, fixes the conventions used throughout the site, and shows the step that makes all
three geometries tractable: separation of variables, which turns the vector field problem into a scalar second-order
ordinary differential equation in one coordinate. The next section explains why that equation is solved, in every
geometry, by a $2\times 2$ transfer matrix.

## Maxwell's equations in a piecewise homogeneous medium

The media on this site are **linear, isotropic and piecewise homogeneous**: the stack, the cylinder and the sphere are
made of regions in which the relative permittivity $\varepsilon$ and permeability $\mu$ are constants, separated by
sharp interfaces. Inside each region, with no free charges or currents, Maxwell's equations read

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D} = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0, \qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, \qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t},
$$

with the constitutive relations $\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0\varepsilon\,\mathbf{E}$ and
$\mathbf{B} = \mu_0\mu\,\mathbf{H}$.

**The time convention.** Every field is monochromatic with the time dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$, so a plane wave
travelling along $+z$ is $e^{i(kz - \omega t)}$. With this convention an absorbing medium has a refractive index with a
*positive* imaginary part, $n = n' + i n''$, $n'' \ge 0$, which is how the optical-constant tables on this site list
$n$ and $k$ (the calculator's $k$ is $n''$). Engineers often use $e^{+j\omega t}$ instead, where the same medium has
$n' - j n''$; results carry over by complex conjugation, and the sign of every phase and of $\Delta$ in ellipsometry
flips with it. For harmonic fields the curl equations become

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{E} = i\omega\mu_0\mu\,\mathbf{H}, \qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H} = -i\omega\varepsilon_0\varepsilon\,\mathbf{E},
$$

so that $\mathbf{H}$ is fixed by $\mathbf{E}$ alone: $\mathbf{H} = (i\omega\mu_0\mu)^{-1}\nabla\times\mathbf{E}$.
In each homogeneous region, taking the curl once more gives the vector Helmholtz equation

$$
\nabla\times\nabla\times\mathbf{E} - k^2\mathbf{E} = 0, \qquad k = \frac{\omega}{c}\,n, \qquad n = \sqrt{\varepsilon\mu},
$$

and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = 0$. The vacuum wavenumber is $k_0 = \omega/c = 2\pi/\lambda$, with $\lambda$ the vacuum
wavelength, which is the wavelength every spectrum on this site is plotted against. The wave impedance of a region,
$Z = Z_0\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$, is what distinguishes a magnetic medium from a dielectric of the same $n$; for the
non-magnetic materials that make up almost every example here, $\mu = 1$ and $n = \sqrt{\varepsilon}$.

## The two boundary conditions

At an interface between two regions, integrating Faraday's and Ampère's laws over a vanishing loop that straddles it
gives the conditions every solution must satisfy:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{n}}\times(\mathbf{E}_2 - \mathbf{E}_1) = 0, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{n}}\times(\mathbf{H}_2 - \mathbf{H}_1) = 0 :
$$

**the tangential components of $\mathbf{E}$ and of $\mathbf{H}$ are continuous** (there are no surface currents in a
dielectric or a metal described by a bulk $\varepsilon$). Continuity of the normal components of $\mathbf{D}$ and
$\mathbf{B}$ follows from these two together with the divergence equations and need not be imposed separately. Two
conditions is exactly the number a second-order equation needs, and that count is the whole reason the transfer
matrix exists.

One exception matters on this site. A **two-dimensional sheet**, such as graphene, carries a surface current
$\mathbf{K} = \sigma\,\mathbf{E}_\parallel$ and makes the tangential $\mathbf{H}$ jump by $\hat{\mathbf{n}}\times
\mathbf{K}$; PyStratify models such sheets as a jump condition at the interface rather than as a layer of finite
thickness. A **surface current** is also how an idealised metal is treated in the limit of a perfect conductor.

## Separation of variables: one scalar equation per channel

The vector Helmholtz equation separates in exactly the coordinate systems in which the interfaces of our three
geometries are coordinate surfaces: planes $z = \mathrm{const}$, cylinders $\rho = \mathrm{const}$ and spheres
$r = \mathrm{const}$. In each, the field is a superposition of modes labelled by the quantum numbers of the other two
coordinates, and the dependence on the coordinate normal to the interfaces is a scalar function $\psi$ obeying a
**second-order linear ordinary differential equation**. The three cases are:

| geometry | normal coordinate | channel labels | the equation for $\psi$ | its two independent solutions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| films | $z$ | in-plane wavevector $\mathbf{k}_\parallel$; polarization s or p | $\psi'' + k_z^2\,\psi = 0$, $k_z = \sqrt{k^2 - k_\parallel^2}$ | $e^{\pm i k_z z}$ |
| cylinders | $\rho$ | azimuthal order $m$; axial wavenumber $k_z$ | Bessel's equation, $\rho^2\psi'' + \rho\psi' + (q^2\rho^2 - m^2)\psi = 0$, $q = \sqrt{k^2 - k_z^2}$ | $J_m(q\rho)$, $H^{(1)}_m(q\rho)$ |
| spheres | $r$ | angular momentum $\ell$ (and $m$); electric or magnetic | spherical Bessel's equation, $(r\psi)'' + \left[k^2 - \ell(\ell+1)/r^2\right] r\psi = 0$ | $j_\ell(kr)$, $h^{(1)}_\ell(kr)$ |

The pattern is the same in every row. The first solution is regular (a standing or incoming wave, finite at the centre);
the second is outgoing and singular at the origin, where $h^{(1)}_\ell$ and $H^{(1)}_m$ diverge. In a slab geometry the
same roles are played by waves running towards and away from an interface. Inside region $n$ the field of one channel
is therefore

$$
\psi(x) = A_n\,\psi_+(k_n x) + B_n\,\psi_-(k_n x),
$$

with two unknown amplitudes per region and per channel. The vector field is rebuilt from $\psi$ by the appropriate
vector harmonics: for a film, $\mathbf{E}$ is transverse to the plane of incidence (s, TE) or $\mathbf{H}$ is (p, TM);
for a sphere, the **vector spherical harmonics** $\mathbf{Y}^{(m)}_{\ell m}$, $\mathbf{Y}^{(e)}_{\ell m}$,
$\mathbf{Y}^{(o)}_{\ell m}$ of Jackson and Moroz (or Bohren and Huffman's $\mathbf{M}_{o m \ell}$,
$\mathbf{N}_{e m \ell}$; the two notations give identical results) carry the angular dependence, and each $\ell$
splits into an **electric** (TM) and a **magnetic** (TE) multipole; for a cylinder the orders $m$ carry
$e^{im\varphi}$, and at normal incidence the two polarizations, $\mathbf{E}$ along the axis and $\mathbf{H}$ along it,
decouple exactly as s and p do for a film. The channels are orthogonal, so **each channel is solved on its own**, and
the cross sections and powers are sums over channels with no cross terms.

In the boundary conditions, the continuity of tangential $\mathbf{E}$ becomes the continuity of $\psi$ (up to a known
factor) and the continuity of tangential $\mathbf{H}$, which is proportional to $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}$, becomes the
continuity of a first derivative of $\psi$ weighted by the region's admittance. At each of the $N$ interfaces, each
channel therefore gives **two linear equations**, exactly what is needed to pass from $(A_n, B_n)$ to
$(A_{n+1}, B_{n+1})$.

## Counting the unknowns

For $N$ interfaces there are $N + 1$ regions and $2(N+1)$ amplitudes per channel, and the interfaces supply $2N$
equations. The two missing conditions describe the **source** and the far field:

- **Regularity**: no singular outgoing wave may emerge from the centre of a sphere or the axis of a cylinder unless a
  source sits there, so $B = 0$ in the core. For a film, the equivalent statement is that nothing travels *towards* the
  stack from the far side of the substrate.
- **The incident field**: a plane wave fixes the regular amplitude in the outermost region (for a film, the amplitude
  of the wave arriving from the incident medium). A **point dipole** instead adds a known singular outgoing wave at its
  own position, which is why a dipole problem is the same $2\times 2$ problem with one amplitude shifted, and a
  **focused beam** is a plane wave problem integrated over the angles the objective fills.

The reflected and transmitted waves of a film, the scattering coefficients $a_\ell$, $b_\ell$ of a sphere, and the
$a_m$, $b_m$ of a cylinder are nothing but the remaining amplitudes once the system is solved. From them follow the
far field (reflectance and transmittance; cross sections and the scattering pattern), the near field in every region
(the coefficients *are* the field), the power absorbed in each layer or shell by Poynting's theorem, and, for a
dipole, the power it radiates compared with the same dipole in free space, which is its decay rate.

## Conservation laws as checks

Because the medium is linear and the equations are exact, a lossless structure must satisfy $R + T = 1$ for a film
and $Q_\mathrm{ext} = Q_\mathrm{sca}$ for a particle, and the reciprocity theorem relates a problem to its reverse.
These identities, together with the closed forms of a single interface (the Fresnel equations), a single sphere (Mie's
coefficients) and a single cylinder, are the first lines of the [Verification](verification.html) page: every solver on
this site is checked against them before it is checked against other codes and against papers.

records.title: Why a 2×2 transfer matrix solves every stratified geometry
records.summary: The one idea behind this site's engine: a second-order wave equation has two independent solutions, so the two boundary conditions at an interface always give an invertible 2×2 matrix. Multiplying those matrices across the interfaces solves a film, a coated cylinder or a multilayered sphere with any number of layers, for plane waves and dipoles alike, and the same construction shows where the numerics bite and how PyStratify keeps them stable.

references.cite: F. Abelès, Ann. Phys. (Paris) 12, 596 (1950)
P. Yeh, A. Yariv and C.-S. Hong, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 67, 423 (1977)
A. Moroz, Ann. Phys. 315, 352 (2005)
I. L. Rasskazov, P. S. Carney and A. Moroz, OSA Continuum 3, 2290 (2020)
W. Yang, Appl. Opt. 42, 1710 (2003)
S. J. Byrnes, Multilayer optical calculations, arXiv:1603.02720 (2016)

records.body:
The [previous section](learn/common/maxwell-and-boundary-conditions.html) reduced each geometry to a scalar equation
of the form

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2\Psi}{\mathrm{d}x^2} + k^2(x)\,\Psi = 0
$$

(or its Bessel cousins), with a **piecewise constant** $k$. This section is about the single consequence that makes
the whole site possible: such an equation is solved, in every geometry, by multiplying $2\times 2$ matrices. The
argument takes a paragraph, and it is worth having it clearly in mind, because every later section (the Abelès
matrix of a film, the Mie coefficients of a sphere, the coefficients of a coated cylinder) is one instance of it.

## Two solutions, two conditions, one invertible matrix

A linear second-order equation has exactly two linearly independent solutions in each region, call them $\psi_+$ and
$\psi_-$ (the outgoing and incoming, or regular and singular, waves of the table in the previous section). The field
in region $n$ is

$$
\Psi(x) = A_n\,\psi_+(k_n x) + B_n\,\psi_-(k_n x).
$$

At the interface $x_n$ between regions $n$ and $n+1$ the boundary conditions require continuity of $\Psi$ and of its
"derivative" $\Psi'$ (for electromagnetic waves, of the tangential $\mathbf{E}$ and of the tangential $\mathbf{H}$,
the latter being $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}$ up to an admittance). In matrix form,

$$
\begin{pmatrix} \psi_+(k_n x_n) & \psi_-(k_n x_n) \\ \psi_+'(k_n x_n) & \psi_-'(k_n x_n) \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} A_n \\ B_n \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} \psi_+(k_{n+1} x_n) & \psi_-(k_{n+1} x_n) \\ \psi_+'(k_{n+1} x_n) & \psi_-'(k_{n+1} x_n) \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} A_{n+1} \\ B_{n+1} \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The determinant of either matrix is the **Wronskian** $W(\psi_+, \psi_-) = \psi_+\psi_-' - \psi_+'\psi_-$, and the
Wronskian of two independent solutions of a second-order linear equation is never zero (for $e^{\pm ikx}$ it is
$-2ik$; for the Riccati–Bessel pair $\psi_\ell = x j_\ell$, $\xi_\ell = x h^{(1)}_\ell$ it is $i$). Both matrices are
therefore invertible, by nothing more than Cramer's rule for a $2\times 2$ matrix,

$$
\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix},
$$

and the amplitudes on one side of an interface determine those on the other side **uniquely**, in either direction:

$$
\begin{pmatrix} A_{n+1} \\ B_{n+1} \end{pmatrix} = T^+_n \begin{pmatrix} A_n \\ B_n \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix} A_n \\ B_n \end{pmatrix} = T^-_n \begin{pmatrix} A_{n+1} \\ B_{n+1} \end{pmatrix},
\qquad T^-_n = (T^+_n)^{-1}.
$$

$T^\pm_n$ is the **transfer matrix** of interface $n$. Nothing in this argument depends on the geometry: the moment a
scalar linear second-order wave equation has been identified, a $2\times 2$ transfer-matrix description is not a
convenient choice but the intrinsic structure of the problem.

## Composition: any number of layers for the price of a product

Because the amplitudes of region $n+1$ feed the matrix of interface $n+1$, the matrices of successive interfaces
multiply. **Raising** carries the core's amplitudes outward,

$$
\begin{pmatrix} A_{n} \\ B_{n} \end{pmatrix} = \mathcal{T}(n) \begin{pmatrix} A_1 \\ B_1 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad \mathcal{T}(n) = T^+_{n-1}\,T^+_{n-2}\cdots T^+_1,
$$

and **lowering** carries the outer medium's amplitudes inward with the inverse product. For $N$ interfaces the cost is
$N$ matrix products per channel: linear in the number of layers, with no matrix larger than $2\times 2$ ever formed.
That is why the calculator treats a 50-period Bragg mirror, a nanomatryoshka with four shells and a bare interface
with the same code and the same speed, and why a multilayered sphere is formally **reduced to a homogeneous one**:
the composite matrix $\mathcal{T}(N+1)$ plays, for the whole onion, the role the single-interface matrix plays for
Mie's sphere, and the cross sections keep Mie's form with composite coefficients.

In the planar case the product is Abelès' 1950 construction. Written for the tangential fields rather than for
the amplitudes it is the **characteristic matrix** of a layer, $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\delta & (i/\eta)\sin\delta \\
i\eta\sin\delta & \cos\delta\end{pmatrix}$, whose product over the layers gives the admittance of a coating; the
[transfer-matrix section](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html) for films develops it. For a periodic stack Yeh, Yariv
and Hong showed that the eigenvalues of the unit cell's matrix decide whether a wave propagates or is stopped, which
is the band structure of a Bragg mirror. For spheres the same products are the recursive algorithm of the
[multilayered sphere](learn/spheres/recursive-transfer-matrix.html); for cylinders, of the
[coated cylinder](learn/cylinders/infinite-cylinder.html).

## Closing the system: the two conditions that are not at an interface

The products relate the $2(N+1)$ amplitudes by $2N$ equations. The remaining two are the physics of the source:

- **Regularity at the centre** (or no wave from beyond the substrate): $B_1 = 0$ for a sphere or cylinder with the
  source outside. The field in the core is then a regular wave of unknown amplitude $A_1$.
- **The incident field**: the regular amplitude in the outermost region is the known plane wave, $A_{N+1} = 1$ in the
  natural normalisation. The outgoing amplitude $B_{N+1}$ is the scattered wave: it is what $\mathcal{T}$ returns, and
  it *is* the Mie coefficient of order $\ell$ (or the Fresnel reflection coefficient, or the cylinder's $a_m$).

A **point dipole** changes only this last step: it adds a known outgoing wave in the region where it sits, so the
amplitudes jump by a prescribed amount at the dipole's radius, and the two conditions become regularity at the centre
and *no incoming wave from infinity*. The same matrices, built once for the structure, then give the fields of a plane
wave, of a dipole anywhere inside or outside, and, by integrating plane waves over a cone, of a focused beam. The
calculator's three sources share one solver for exactly this reason.

## What the matrix gives for free

Since the amplitudes $(A_n, B_n)$ in every region are produced along the way, the transfer matrix returns not just the
far field but the **field everywhere**: the standing-wave pattern inside a filter, the field at the surface of a
sphere where a molecule sits, the power dissipated in each shell (from Poynting's theorem applied region by region).
The channels remain separate, so each multipole's share of the scattering, each polarization's reflectance and each
guided mode's power are read off without any further work. These are the per-layer absorptance, the multipole
decomposition and the emission channels the calculator displays.

## Where it bites, and how PyStratify stays stable

The construction is exact in arithmetic of infinite precision. In floating point two things go wrong, and both are
visible in the matrices above.

1. **Growing exponentials.** In an absorbing layer, or where a wave is evanescent (beyond the critical angle, inside a
   metal, in a sphere's high-order channels where $|m|x \gg \ell$), one of the two solutions grows exponentially across
   the region. The transfer matrix carries both, so its elements grow like $e^{+|k''|d}$ and overflow for a thick metal
   or a large sphere, long before the physics does anything unusual; worse, subtracting two huge numbers to recover a
   small reflected amplitude loses every significant digit. The remedies are all variations on one theme: never
   propagate the growing solution explicitly. Scattering-matrix (Redheffer star-product) formulations only ever combine
   decaying exponentials; Byrnes' planar code, which `pystratify.planar` descends from, does the same for films; for
   spheres and cylinders PyStratify carries the amplitudes together with their **logarithms**, so that the
   Riccati–Bessel functions of complex argument, which grow like $e^{|\mathrm{Im}\, z|}$, are scaled out before any
   product is formed. The sections on the [multilayered sphere](learn/spheres/recursive-transfer-matrix.html) describe
   the recursion that results (Moroz 2005; Yang 2003; Rasskazov, Carney and Moroz 2020).
2. **Truncation.** The sum over channels is infinite. For spheres the series converges once $\ell$ exceeds the size
   parameter by a few terms (Wiscombe's $\ell_\mathrm{max} = x + 4x^{1/3} + 2$), but a high-index core, a thin metal
   shell or a dipole close to the surface needs more, because the field it radiates is rich in high orders;
   PyStratify therefore raises the order to cover the largest internal size parameter and, for emitters, until the
   rate converges. Keeping orders is cheap; dropping them silently is how a code reproduces Mie's figures and still
   gets a quenching curve wrong.

Both points are tested, not assumed: the [Verification](verification.html) page lists the extended-precision
references (the same recursion in 60-digit arithmetic), the independent codes and the closed forms against which every
geometry's transfer matrices are checked.

verification.title: How PyStratify is verified
verification.summary: Every check behind multilayer.app's engine, geometry by geometry and source by source: closed forms, extended-precision references, independent methods, other groups' codes and published papers, each with its script, its tolerance and whether it runs on every test.
verification.body:
The calculator computes every film, cylinder and sphere with PyStratify, an open-source Python package (GPL-3.0).
This page lists what PyStratify is checked against. One row is one comparison: a reference, the quantity compared,
the script that runs it, the tolerance it must meet and whether the test suite asserts it on every change.

A check counts as independent only when the reference shares no code with PyStratify. Closed forms and conservation
laws are independent of any code; extended-precision references prove the numerics; another group's code or a
different method (finite differences in time, finite elements, boundary elements, volume integrals) proves the
formulation. Every comparison is a script in the PyStratify repository, so anyone can rerun it and see the numbers;
the rows marked *suite* run on every commit.

Rows the calculator can open show a worked example; the switch at the top shows one geometry at a time.

kinds.proves: a closed form, limit or conservation law: independent of any code
the same mathematics in mpmath at 60–80 digits, written separately in `src/pystratify/references.py` and `benchmarks/mp_reference.py`: proves the numerics, not the formulation
an independent formulation inside this repo (a scattering matrix, a plane-wave superposition, a quadrature): proves the formulation

a code that shares PyStratify's ancestry. `planar.py` *is* Byrnes's `tmm` (MIT notice in `src/pystratify/PLANAR-LICENSE.txt`); the backend's `inc_tmm`/"GTMM" path descends from it (so did the site's JavaScript `tutorial-engine.js`, removed 2026-10-11). Agreement is a regression check only

statuses.meaning: asserted on every `pytest` run in this repo; rows marked "`benchmarks` extra" need `pip install -e ".[test,benchmarks]"` and run in the CI job `benchmarks`
scored per record by `harvester/verify.py`; not asserted
regenerated by `python benchmarks/convergence.py` into `RESULTS.md` (or `planar_codes.py` into `PLANAR_CODES.md`); not asserted
a `crosscheck/` script that writes CSV and PNG to lay over a published figure; agreement read by eye
not yet written; the row names what to compare and the tolerance to aim for
ruled out, with the reason in the row

rows: Meep (FDTD; cylindrical coordinates where the source is on axis)
Majic & Le Ru 2020; Yuan, Zhu & Zhu 2023/24; Wu et al. 1991/1997
classic papers recomputed (`crosscheck/classics/`, 16; the site's Classics page)

verification.findings:
- **Where the remaining `to build` rows stand (2026-10-11).** Every code comparison PyStratify can run alone is
  built. The classic papers (`crosscheck/classics/`, 16 scripts, every toleranced check passing) now cover the
  paper rows for OLED emitters (Neyts), Bohren & Huffman's cylinder, FT-IR fibres (Davis 2011), Kerker and
  nanoshells (Fu, Prodan) and Anger–Novotny quenching. Still to build: Furno's OLEDs, Davis 2010's film, a nanowire
  emitter, an FT-IR sphere paper and Oldenburg's nanoshells (WP1.6, with the classics' second wave); pyElli 4×4, PyMoosh `anisotropic.py` and the isotropic
  limit wait for WP1.4's anisotropic solver; PyMoosh `non_local.py` waits for the `non-local` merge;
  OpenSANS needs its CPC program library download.

- **Films now have two independent codes** (2026-10-10): PyMoosh and pyElli agree with
  `pystratify.planar` to ≤ 1.2e-14 in R, T, r, t and per-layer A, and to ≤ 6e-13° in Ψ and Δ, including
  opaque and 20 µm absorbing layers, total internal reflection and a magnetic layer
  (`PLANAR_CODES.md`). Plane-wave fields agree with PyMoosh to ≤ 1.6e-14, and every guided mode of
  four lossless guides with PyMoosh (≤ 1.1e-11) and the slab dispersion relation (≤ 6.6e-14).
  Conventions that had to be mapped: PyMoosh's p-polarised t is the H-field ratio, and pyElli's
  Δ = 180° − Δ(tmm). Still open on films: anisotropy (pyElli's 4×4, with WP1.4).
- **Film emitter rates now have two outside references** (2026-10-10): independently written
  Sommerfeld integrals, pinned to the image-dipole closed form, agree with `FilmSource` to ≤ 5e-12;
  smuthi agrees on lossless guides to ≤ 4.8e-7. The guide comparison **found a bug**: a source in an
  exterior half-space lost all guided power (fixed in 0.10.3). **Cylinder emitters have an outside
  reference since 2026-10-10**: Meep's 3D FDTD converges toward PyStratify (0.74% at 60 px/µm, every
  orientation, through a mode cutoff), and its first run **found a bug**: the guided-mode search dropped
  real modes while reporting convergence (up to 12% here, 9.5% over random cylinders; fixed in 0.10.4,
  the found modes now equal the fibre's closed-form dispersion relations). NGSolve's 3D finite
  elements are the second volume method (1.5% at 0.8 µm; a mode just above cutoff needs a larger cell
  than 8 GB allows).
- **Volume methods (FDTD, FEM, BEM) are a different-method check at ~1%**, not a precision check:
  they test the formulation (sign conventions, normalisation, multipole bookkeeping), not the digits.
  Meep in cylindrical coordinates is cheap for a dipole on the symmetry axis: since 2026-10-10 a sphere
  agrees to 1.7% and a guiding film to 3.7% at 100 px/µm (2D, under a minute each); off-axis sources and
  cylinders need 3D runs, one at a time on this 8 GB Mac. At 200 px/µm Meep's E_z (m = 0) runs jump at the
  band's lowest frequency (+9% sphere, +12% film) while everything else keeps converging — Meep-side,
  noted in the report, not yet explained.
- **Spheres are the best covered**: precision, BHMIE, five papers, and since 2026-10-10 two Mie codes run
  publicly (scattnlay and treams agree with PyStratify to ≤ 1.8e-11 once 20 orders beyond Wiscombe's
  truncation are kept; at the default truncation, what a user gets, to ≤ 3.7e-8) and a
  different *method*: MNPBEM's boundary elements converge toward PyStratify for cross sections and
  decay rates (`MNPBEM_SPHERES.md`), and pyGDM2's volume dipoles agree within ~3% for dielectric
  spheres (`GDM_SPHERES.md`). A 5 nm nanoshell is beyond MNPBEM's affordable meshes here; three
  Mie codes (PyStratify, treams, scattnlay) settle that case exactly. **Near fields** too
  (2026-10-10): E and H inside every layer and outside agree with scattnlay to ≤ 8.2e-13 and the
  scattered field with treams to ≤ 6.6e-14; the centre is exact (Bohren & Huffman's d₁, c₁ to
  1e-14), where scattnlay loses up to 5e-3, and scattnlay's internal field fails toward the core of a
  10-layer sphere whose PyStratify coefficients agree with 60-digit transfer matrices. **Emitters**
  beside a sphere agree with smuthi to machine precision (2.2e-16) for dielectric spheres and to
  5e-10 for a metal-like sphere 5 nm away, converging with smuthi's truncation; beside **layered**
  spheres (a nanoshell, a matryoshka; electric and magnetic dipoles) with treams, to 3e-15 for
  dielectric shells and 3e-8 / 1e-11 for the metal ones; Meep (cylindrical coordinates) agrees to 1.7%.
- **Focused beams are verified only against their own plane-wave engines.** The FT-IR papers are
  the outside check.
- **The incoherent film path** has only the explicit phase average as an independent check. The
  backend's "GTMM" comparison is `inc_tmm` itself. PyMoosh's `incoherent.py` is now the outside
  check for a thick incoherent substrate; stacks with several incoherent layers are still unchecked.
- **PyMoosh covers the most planar cells of any one code**: R/T/A and fields, incoherent stacks,
  anisotropy, dipole sources, guided modes and hydrodynamic films. `benchmarks/planar_codes.py` is
  where its next cells go.

fresnel-oblique.note: Brewster's angle, where R_p vanishes, is arctan(1.5) = 56.3°; the two curves coincide to machine precision at every angle.

airy-slab.title: A 300 nm slab of n = 2 in air at normal incidence: the Airy formula
airy-slab.note: R = F sin²δ / (1 + F sin²δ) with F = 4R₁/(1 − R₁)², R₁ the single-surface reflectance and δ = 2πnd/λ: the fringes of a Fabry–Pérot slab.

energy-conservation.title: A lossless five-layer stack lit from glass, through the critical angle: 1 − R − T
energy-conservation.note: Beyond the critical angle (41.1° in this glass) T is exactly zero and R is exactly one; the residual is floating-point rounding, floored at 10⁻¹⁷ for the logarithmic axis.

sommerfeld-film-emitter.title: A dipole in air above 60 nm of silver on glass, 633 nm: PyStratify against the Sommerfeld integrals
sommerfeld-film-emitter.note: The reference integrates the Chance–Prock–Silbey integrands with Parratt's recursion for r_s and r_p, written without PyStratify; quenching rises as d⁻³ at contact and the surface plasmon of the silver sets the breakpoint of the evanescent integral.

mie-homogeneous.title: A homogeneous sphere, m = 1.5: Mie's series, one shell and fifty identical shells
mie-homogeneous.note: The textbook coefficients a_ℓ, b_ℓ (Riccati–Bessel functions from SciPy) summed directly, against the transfer-matrix recursion with one interface and with fifty interfaces between identical media.

bhmie-large-spheres.title: Large absorbing spheres, m = 1.5 + 0.1i: PyStratify against BHMIE to x = 5000
bhmie-large-spheres.note: BHMIE's downward recurrence for the logarithmic derivative, ported from the book's Appendix A, against the logarithmic transfer-matrix recursion, both summed 20 orders beyond Wiscombe's truncation; the x axis is logarithmic and the extinction tends to 2 with the ripple of the edge waves. For a weakly absorbing or lossless sphere BHMIE's double-precision recurrence drifts at large x (3e-4 in Q_ext at x = 1481 for m = 1.33 + 1e-4 i, 6e-4 for m = 1.33), where PyStratify agrees with the same series summed in 40-digit arithmetic (pystratify.references.sphere_extinction) to 2e-13: the absorbing case here is the one the test suite asserts.

sixty-digit-coefficients.title: A 5 nm metal nanoshell on a 15 nm silica core, 600 nm: Mie coefficients against 60-digit transfer matrices
sixty-digit-coefficients.note: T_ℓ = B_host / A_host of the regular solution: the scattered amplitude of each order. The coefficients fall over fifty decades across the orders shown; double precision follows the 60-digit evaluation of the same recursion all the way down.

treams-nanoshell.title: A nanoshell (10 nm silica core, 10 nm shell of ε = −10 + i): PyStratify against treams
treams-nanoshell.note: treams (Beutel et al.) builds the T-matrix of a layered sphere from its own vector spherical waves; the fixed metal index keeps the shell's plasmon at one wavelength, so the comparison is of the two codes, not of a material.

sphere-decay-mpmath.title: A dipole beside a 25 nm sphere of m = 0.05 + 3.5i at 600 nm: decay rates against the 40-digit series
sphere-decay-mpmath.worst_label: largest relative difference over the four rates
sphere-decay-mpmath.note: Chew's sums over 400 orders in mpmath at 40 digits against PyStratify's adaptive order and logarithmic amplitudes; the total rate climbs as d⁻³ at contact (quenching) while the radiative rate stays finite.

treams-dipole-nanoshell.title: A dipole 5–60 nm from a nanoshell (10 nm silica core, 10 nm shell of ε = −10 + i), 600 nm: PyStratify against treams
treams-dipole-nanoshell.note: treams translates the dipole's ℓ = 1 singular wave to the sphere's centre, scatters it with the T-matrix (50 orders; closer than 5 nm its truncation no longer converges, PyStratify's adaptive order does) and reads the scattered field back at the dipole; PyStratify places the jump in its transfer-matrix recursion.

treams-cylinder-oblique.title: A cylinder of radius 100 nm, n = 1.5 + 0.01i, at 60° to its axis: cross widths against treams
treams-cylinder-oblique.note: Oblique incidence couples the two polarizations at the surface; both codes average the two incident polarizations. treams' cylindrical T-matrix is per axial wavenumber, which a plane wave fixes.

cylinder-bessel-direct.title: A cylinder of n = 1.5 in air at 600 nm, normal incidence: the coefficients from the Bessel boundary equations

series.label: E along the axis, Bessel equations
H along the axis, Bessel equations

cylinder-bessel-direct.note: Each order's coefficient solved directly from the two boundary conditions in SciPy's Bessel functions (Bohren & Huffman §8.4), summed into Q_sca = (2/x) Σ|t_m|², against the cylinder transfer matrices.

fibre-dispersion.title: A step-index fibre, n = 2, radius 150 nm, in air: guided modes against the dispersion relations
fibre-dispersion.worst_label: largest |n_eff − n_eff(relation)| for TE₀₁ and TM₀₁
fibre-dispersion.note: Snyder & Love's TE₀₁ and TM₀₁ relations, J₁(u)/(u J₀(u)) + c K₁(w)/(w K₀(w)) = 0, solved by bisection, against the poles PyStratify finds behind a dipole's guided channel; HE₁₁ (no closed form of this kind, and no cutoff) is shown as found; the shorter wavelengths guide higher modes too, not drawn. TE₀₁ and TM₀₁ reach cutoff at 0.392 µm, where V = 2.405.
